19. ID: 6598
   Year: 2002
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: The Danish Organisation for Renewable Energy
   Statement: Our position is that wind turbine financing has become a standard offering in the portfolios of several banks, which view it as a low-risk investment comparable to real estate. Financing conditions differ based on whether an investor is purchasing shares in windpower cooperatives or acquiring an entire wind turbine.  

One bank experienced in windpower financing specifies the following criteria for financing a large turbine with a single investor:  
1. The project must be economically viable, with debt and interest repayment achievable through turbine income within approximately 8 years. This calculation is based on reasonable assumptions about future electricity prices and bonuses and accounts for 90% of the estimated production.  
2. The wind turbine must have guarantees and insurance against defects and production levels below 90% of the estimated output for the first 5 years.  
3. The turbine itself serves as security for the loan.  
4. Income generated by the turbine is directed to the bank for loan servicing, with full repayment targeted within 8 years.  
5. The investor must possess free capital equivalent to 20% of the investment. However, loans can cover up to 100% of the investment if repayment within the 8-year timeframe is feasible.

21. ID: 6596
   Year: 2002
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: The Danish Organisation for Renewable Energy
   Statement: Our position is that the siting of wind turbines is an integral component of Danish land-use planning. In 1994, all municipalities were tasked with designating sites for wind turbine groups and parks. By 1999, the responsibility for revising these plans was transferred to counties as part of their regional planning processes.  

This system of designated sites streamlined the installation of wind turbines, significantly facilitating development for wind power developers during the 1990s. However, as most of these designated sites were utilized during that period, the installation of new wind turbines now often requires the designation of additional sites. This process involves a more extended planning procedure, including conducting an Environmental Impact Assessment, which adds complexity to wind energy development.

22. ID: 1951
   Year: 2002
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Dominic Machaelis
   Statement: Wind energy at sea is at its strongest, unaffected by land masses. The Energy Island has six large aerogenerators, three at a lower height (OMIT) to intercept the sea-hugging wind flow, while three are at greater heights to capture the upper wind flows. The hydraulic masts are able to adjust the heights of the aerogenerators to best harvest the wind potential from different directions.

Apart from its electricity contribution, the Energy Island is designed also to produce hydrogen. Because of the fluctuation of renewable energy resources, an energy storage system is required. The Energy Island relies on a hydrolysis plant to produce stored hydrogen and oxygen, part of which can be used by fuel cell technology as necessary to balance the power output for both external and internal uses. Part of the fuel can, in some cases, be tankered or pipelined to other destinations, when the electricity produced is not totally used by cable links to nearby destinations.

The Energy Island will also produce a base for Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA) and Mariculture. In tropical latitudes, greenhouses need to be protected from the sun, a role performed by the heliostats, and well ventilated or evaporatively cooled. The 22-hectare platform can therefore be used for CEA, using part of the distilled water from the open OTEC cycle for hydroponics. If the floor is trellised, light can reach the seawater below, where pens would contain various forms of marine life.

Harbours and Housing: On the leeward side of the island or islands, the Energy Island needs to provide housing for staff, social facilities, workshops and harbours.

The Energy Island uses many diverse renewable energy sources, bringing their converted powers together in the most efficient way to provide electricity for the grid, and, by hydrolysis, hydrogen fuel for transport to nearby or distant population centers, where it can be used efficiently by fuel cell technology. The Energy Island can become a major supplier of electricity and hydrogen fuel for a pollution free society, and liberate the world from the perils of nuclear power generation, and from its political, economic and polluting dependence on dwindling fossil fuels. The Energy Island therefore constitutes a new departure, demonstrated to be all the more necessary by the visible signs of pollution and global warming, and the frightening fact that world energy use is expanding exponentially, having doubled in the last thirty years. Action is needed to bring about change and turn the tide.

34. ID: 5720
   Year: 2006
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Vladislav Akhmatov , Hans Knudsen
   Statement: We observe that the Danish power system is shifting from centralized power plants to dispersed generation, including local CHP units and large offshore wind farms. This transition reduces reliance on centralized plants for voltage and frequency control, presenting challenges for maintaining grid stability. Currently, centralized plants are essential for stabilizing the grid during faults, as dispersed generation frequently disconnects under such conditions.

To address these challenges, we ensure that offshore wind farms comply with grid requirements, including ride-through capabilities. Fixed-speed turbines utilize blade-angle control to minimize power during faults, while variable-speed turbines rely on crowbar protection and pitch control. These technologies play a critical role in stabilizing turbines during faults but still depend on centralized plants to re-establish grid stability. Drawing from these experiences, we aim to inform the design and operation of a future power system with a growing share of wind power.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

37. ID: 5723
   Year: 2007
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jacob Ladenburg
   Statement: I analyzed the Danish population's attitudes toward increasing on-land wind turbines and offshore wind farms. The results show that the population generally has a positive attitude toward wind power. Specifically, attitudes are influenced by characteristics such as age (negative correlation), gender, experience with offshore wind farms, and beach usage. Notably, whether respondents can see wind turbines from their homes or summer houses does not significantly affect their attitudes.

The survey reveals a clear preference for offshore wind farms over on-land turbines, suggesting that future wind power development should prioritize offshore projects. However, on-land development remains a feasible and cost-effective alternative, particularly if smaller turbines are replaced with fewer, larger ones, improving efficiency and public acceptance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

38. ID: 1894
   Year: 2007
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: PlanEnergi
   Statement: We believe the Samsø Energy Island project must be regarded as a near-complete success. Our primary objective—achieving 100% self-sufficiency with renewable energy using local resources—has been accomplished. This achievement includes the total elimination of CO₂ emissions and other air pollutants. A key factor behind this success is the active mobilization and support of the local community, who embraced and adopted the project.

However, not all conservation objectives have been met. In particular, goals related to heating and electricity efficiency were not fully achieved, and transportation remains largely unchanged, still dependent on non-renewable energy sources.

This project was an enormous undertaking for a small community, yet they completed it on schedule. But could the same be done on a national scale? There are significant challenges to consider. National energy consumption per capita is 25% higher than that of Samsø. Additionally, Denmark has only one-third of the biomass resources per capita compared to Samsø, and the national wind resource potential per person is also lower.

If Samsø’s contribution is viewed as part of Denmark's national renewable energy (RE) supply, two scenarios emerge:

If based on Samsø’s land and resource capacity, RE production would need to increase fourfold.
If based on Samsø’s population proportion, RE production must increase by 25%.
In either case, a significant increase in renewable energy production would be required. These observations are not intended to diminish Samsø’s achievements but to provide perspective on the scale of a national transition to renewable energy.

One crucial conclusion is clear: if Denmark aims to make a similar transition, substantial energy conservation efforts are necessary to reduce overall energy consumption. Samsø’s experience demonstrates that these savings will not happen automatically—it will require substantial effort, supported by economic incentives and penalties. Importantly, every kilowatt-hour saved is more valuable than one produced—it requires no maintenance or service.

A direct application of Samsø’s results to Denmark indicates that transitioning to a renewable energy system nationwide would require an investment of approximately 670 billion DKK (89 billion EUR). However, this transition could yield annual savings of around 60 billion DKK (8 billion EUR), allowing the investment to pay off in just 11 years—a promising return, given the gravity of the challenge and the potential benefits.

   Statement: The Danish Energy Island projects aimed to showcase how local areas could achieve 100% renewable energy self-sufficiency using available technologies and fostering strong community involvement. Samsø Island's approach, which won the 1997 competition, succeeded due to a practical and detailed master plan that balanced technical feasibility, local participation, and innovative organizational models. The plan emphasized reducing energy consumption across heating, electricity, and transportation sectors while leveraging existing resources and technologies. Ten years after its initiation, the Samsø project demonstrated notable progress, although adjustments to original estimates and methodologies highlighted initial data inaccuracies. The ongoing transition continues to yield new initiatives, demonstrating Samsø's commitment to renewable energy leadership and its role as a global showcase for Danish renewable energy technology.

43. ID: 780
   Year: 2008
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ina Jakobsen
   Statement: As Ina Jakobsen of Oslo University, I observe that Samsø's status as the Renewable Energy Island has positively impacted the local economy in several ways. Firstly, these projects have generated new employment opportunities. Specifically, the planning and implementation of the wind turbine and heating projects created approximately 20 jobs annually between 1998 and 2007. Local craftsmen have gained employment through these initiatives. Furthermore, the Energy Academy and other institutions involved in the planning process have generated numerous additional jobs. Secondly, the projects have stimulated the tourist sector. While Samsø has historically been a tourist destination due to its natural beauty, the Renewable Energy Island project has fostered a new form of tourism: professional tourism. Politicians, business representatives, grassroots organizations, media outlets, and students from around the globe visit Samsø to observe the organization and implementation of these renewable energy projects.

44. ID: 781
   Year: 2008
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ina Jakobsen
   Statement: The concept of social acceptance can be discussed as the term implies that there is a need for people to accept the technology, but it does not imply any further involvement. This in turn shows a top-down attitude towards wind energy implementation where it becomes important for decision-makers to make people accept the technology and the implementation of it. This is problematic as a bottom-up development of wind energy projects is highlighted here as one of the keys to ensure project success. It may be contradictory to speak of the importance of bottom-up initiative and local participation on the one hand and acceptance on the other. However, the concept does provide some useful insight especially as in acceptance versus opposition. The concept will be used in this thesis with this purpose and without implying that acceptance exclude local participation. Rather, further involvement by the local community will be emphasized as a necessary key to in fact ensure acceptance. However, I will emphasize that the concept of social acceptance is a dynamic process. There can be different levels of social acceptance. Different actors and stakeholders may have different incentives for participation and thus different levels of acceptance. A wind energy project includes environmental, social and economic aspects, and the challenge is to find a way to make sure all these aspects and interests are integrated in the same project.

57. ID: 5719
   Year: 2009
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jochen Markard ,  Regula Petersen
   Statement: Offshore wind power has transformed the wind energy sector by leveraging open sea space and strong wind speeds for large-scale electricity generation. However, it is a capital-intensive and technologically demanding industry, requiring financial and organizational resources that exclude many smaller investors. Our analysis of offshore wind park ownership in Denmark, the UK, and Germany reveals that large firms, particularly from the electricity sector, dominate investments. In Denmark and the UK, oil and gas industry players also play a significant role in offshore wind development. 

This marks a major shift for countries like Germany and Denmark, where the wind power sector initially thrived on investments from individuals, farmers, cooperatives, and independent developers. The rise of offshore wind thus signifies a transition toward market concentration and a departure from the inclusive investment model that previously characterized these countries' renewable energy landscapes.

73. ID: 6591
   Year: 2011
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: US Department of Energy (DOE)
   Statement: Our position is that six key applications are suitable for large-scale energy storage systems exceeding 100 MW capacity. These applications include:  

1. Electric Energy Time-shift  
2. Electric Supply Capacity  
3. Load Following  
4. Renewable Energy Time-shift  
5. Renewable Capacity Firming, with durations ranging from 15 to 60 minutes and 60 to 120 minutes  
6. Wind Generation Grid Integration for long-duration storage  

Applications best suited for bulk energy storage are characterized by long discharge durations (measured in hours), frequent usage, deep discharge depths, and response times within a few minutes. Additionally, these applications require a minimum cycle life of several thousand cycles.  

We evaluated the technical requirements of these applications against novel energy storage technologies to determine their ability to meet these needs effectively. This comparison focuses on ensuring alignment between the demands of these applications and the capabilities of the emerging technologies.

101. ID: 812
   Year: 2014
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Hongda Liu, Lei Zhou
   Statement: We suggest a self-reconfiguration strategy to improve the energy extraction of island renewable energy sources. This strategy is implemented by means of a controllable matrix of switches configuring the photovoltaic modules in a single-string of parallel-connected rows connected to the converter. A set of simulation results carried out under a proof of concept basis on a small-scale grid-connected photovoltaic system has shown both the feasibility of the approach and the resulting improvement of the delivered power under partial shades or in case of cells failure. The power loss mitigation of this approach can result interesting for small-scale installations in island environments where the photovoltaic cells can work under conditions of severe partial shadows or fault conditions projected by surrounding obstacles or extreme weather like storms and plum rains. As a result, the photovoltaic system exhibits a self-capacity for real-time adaptation to the photovoltaic cell external operating conditions and improves the energy extraction of the system.

103. ID: 774
   Year: 2015
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Mathilde Drouineau, Edi Assoumou, Vincent Mazauric, Nadia Maïzi
   Statement: The study -Increasing shares of intermittent sources in Reunion Island: Impacts on the future reliability of power supply- enables us to draw three main conclusions:
• Electricity autonomy is achievable by 2030 with the available renewable energy sources potentials in the island. The three renewable scenarios, which prohibit fossil fuels, can indeed fulfill the electricity consumption, even considering a large development of electrical vehicles. The results show that the electricity autonomy can only be achieved thanks to high levels of biomass production, which represent at least half of the total production by 2030. It also leads to high shares in the production mixes: in 2030, these scenarios exhibit several hours by day where photovoltaics represent from 40% to two thirds of the instantaneous electricity production.
• However, we observe that the reliability indicators decrease over the time horizon, thus revealing that reliability of power supply will be damaged with high levels of intermittent sources. This also explains why fuel oil׳s power plants appear as back-up units when facing high shares of intermittency even though they do not produce electricity in the results. Since the use of fossil fuels is prohibited in 2030, the reliability of power supply will actually be worsen in scenarios that aim at electricity autonomy, as long as reliability is not addressed properly.
• Finally, results also show that it is possible to restore the reliability of supply when enforcing the legal limit of 30% of intermittent sources in the instantaneous production. This result consequently provides a generation mix that both complies with the electricity autonomy target and with a satisfying reliability of power supply, provided that appropriate rules on the instantaneous production are defined. Furthermore, impacts on reliability of supply and subsequent overcosts of storage devices or changes in consumption patterns induced with demand response should also be investigated. This can be achieved by endogenizing the reliability of future power production mixes in TIMES models to consider appropriate investments preventing from decreasing reliability of power supply.

111. ID: 5757
   Year: 2015
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Til Kristian Vrana
   Statement: The electrical installations for offshore wind power plants are currently built above sea level. We know that the necessary substructure for a transformer or converter platform becomes more costly with increasing water depth and mass. Therefore, we believe the main challenges are the hydrostatic pressure, the rough sea environment, and the extreme reliability requirements, as maintenance is very complicated at the seabed. Subsea technology has not been seen as crucially important for offshore wind, where water depths are usually less than 50m. However, we believe that subsea technology might find its way into the offshore wind sector, possibly leading to transformer stations or even converter stations being placed on the seabed. Therefore, we find it necessary to investigate the possibilities and potentials of the subsea approach.

As we have observed a steadily increasing share of HVDC components in the European power grid, making this approach is becoming outdated. 
We propose that control philosophies for hybrid AC+DC grids have to be developed, as these can address the future reality much better than the classical AC approach. We think the North Sea region with its very high concentration of HVDC infrastructure is a perfect case for studying hybrid AC+DC grid control. We believe the North Sea region will significantly benefit from improved operational principles.

We know that protection of large HVDC systems is challenging. Protection schemes including fast fault location for selective fault clearing are still work in progress. In the report we have illustrated two different approaches: adapting AC protection strategies to work for DC (TRL3-5) or completely new DC power system protection (TRL 1-3). The protection components, both circuit breakers and fault current limiters, are immature at the moment. Although we know HVDC breaker prototypes have been successfully developed, the performance has never been tested in a real HVDC system, which will be a challenge. We believe the optimal HVDC converter control in case of a DC fault is not yet known and possibly depends on converter topology. We find the design of the complex protection system needs further development, before implementation. We urge the stakeholders to investigate alternative protection concepts compared to the classical AC-inspired protection approaches.

We believe low Frequency AC (LFAC) technology has to be further studied with regards to its use for integrating medium-distance offshore wind power plants. For near-shore WPPs (less than ca. 100 km from shore), we believe regular AC is normally the best choice, and for remote offshore WPPs (more than ca. 100 km from shore) we believe DC is usually the best choice. 
For WPPs with an intermediate distance (ca. 50-150 km from shore) we believe LFAC might offer benefits, then the two already mentioned options. We find that LFAC approach also poses a serious threat for the establishment of a future North Sea Super Grid, as it pushes the limits of how far offshore we can go with AC technology. We have showcased in this report that many of the future offshore wind power plants needs to be integrated with LFAC instead of HVDC, as the number of HVDC connected facilities is reduced. We believe a smaller total number of relevant facilities might reduce the incentives and benefits to consider a HVDC based North Sea Super Grid.

We found during our investigation of that operating and controlling HVDC connected isolated offshore AC systems is challenging, as these are highly important for offshore supernodes and therefore can be an enabler for the NSSG. Present offshore grid studies have focused on grid topologies and detailed cable planning. However, we believe that integrated storage has not been considered enough in this context. We see a need for more research within these areas specific on the added value of placing storage units offshore and considering placement in a meshed grid HVDC structure. We think it would be a very large step to take the decision to now build a full-scale North Sea Super Grid, as more investigation into its constructed is needed as outlined in this report.

159. ID: 5732
   Year: 2016
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Researchers
   Statement: The offshore grid has unique technical, economic, and social characteristics, requiring different research methodologies for various questions. Net social benefits at a regional level generally increase with higher offshore wind capacities and more integrated grids. The grid can provide benefits such as more efficient dispatch, better wind power connection, increased system flexibility and reliability, and interconnection of power markets and Nordic storage.

A meshed grid typology may enhance these benefits compared to a radial one, requiring less investment and reducing offshore wind curtailment, along with other non-monetary benefits. However, a meshed grid without proper cost and benefit allocation creates winners and losers among North Seas countries and their neighbors. The offshore grid involves unproven technology, especially control strategies and large HVDC breakers, and an integrated grid could require greater investments than a radial one.

There are significant technical, governance, and regulatory challenges for a meshed grid, which in some studies show only marginally greater benefits than a radial solution. Studies indicate the offshore grid will develop gradually, starting with national shared transmission and bilateral interconnector projects, followed by international pilot projects, and eventually more complex ones.

203. ID: 2380
   Year: 2017
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Benjamin Kroposki
   Statement: Integrating high levels of Variable Renewable Energy (VRE), like wind and solar power, into the electricity grid is a significant technical challenge. These challenges arise from the inherent variability and uncertainty of these resources, as well as their impact on grid stability due to their asynchronous nature.

To address these challenges, I believe a multi-pronged approach is necessary. Geographic diversification of renewable energy sources across different regions can help smooth out fluctuations in production. Using flexible power plants, such as natural gas plants that can quickly adjust their output to compensate for changes in VRE generation, is also crucial. I also think it’s important to implement strategies to control electricity demand, like encouraging customers to shift energy consumption to times of high renewable energy production. In some cases, I know it might even be necessary to temporarily curtail VRE generation when production exceeds grid demand.

Dealing with the uncertainty associated with VRE requires continuous improvements in weather forecasts and VRE production predictions—something I see as essential for effective grid planning and operations. Deploying various energy storage technologies, like batteries, pumped hydro, and compressed air energy storage, is critical to storing excess renewable energy for use during periods of low production.

Ensuring grid stability is paramount, and I think VRE sources—or the energy storage systems associated with them—must be capable of providing essential grid services, like voltage and frequency support, to maintain stability.

In my research, I’ve analyzed real-world examples of grids operating with very high levels of VRE penetration, primarily at smaller scales. What I’ve found is that these systems typically require significant oversizing of VRE capacity and substantial energy storage to ensure reliable grid operation during periods of low renewable energy availability.

These findings, I believe, provide valuable insights for developing large-scale grids with ultra-high levels of VRE penetration. By carefully addressing these challenges and implementing the right solutions, I’m confident we can successfully integrate high levels of renewable energy into our electricity systems while maintaining grid reliability and affordability.

Success depends on supporting local mediators who can bridge the gap between national policy and community needs.

221. ID: 958
   Year: 2017
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Márcia Filipa Oliveira Alves
   Statement: I see the implementation of renewable energy sources (RES) in isolated power systems, such as islands, as both a challenge and an opportunity. In my view, the intermittency of RES creates issues with grid stability and mismatches between power demand and supply. Each power system, in my opinion, must be carefully designed to make the best use of available local resources and create a diverse energy mix. I believe studies like this one are crucial to overcoming these obstacles by improving our understanding of power systems and available RES. They also allow us to create scenarios that maximize RES penetration while evaluating the economic impacts.

I think Pico and Faial Islands, which are close to each other and have similar electricity demands of about 40 GWh/year, are highly dependent on imported fossil fuels and currently rely on wind energy as their primary RES. However, Faial Island faces significant curtailment of wind energy due to grid stability limits. From my perspective, the forestry biomass potential of these islands is substantial enough to meet total demand, but I caution against shifting dependence from fossil fuels to biomass alone.

I propose a scenario that incorporates a mix of wind energy, biomass, urban waste energy, wave energy, hydro power, and solar PV, along with sodium-sulfur batteries as energy storage systems (ESS). Fossil fuel-fired power plants should still play a role in grid stabilization and power backup. My objective is to increase RES penetration in Pico and Faial Islands, reduce fossil fuel dependence, and address urban waste management challenges. The proposed scenario achieves a 12.55 percentage point increase in RES share, raising it to 27.8% and reducing fossil fuel consumption and CO2 emissions by 16.7%. With an optimized ESS capacity of 8 MWh, the RES share could reach 42.3%, reducing fuel oil consumption and CO2 emissions by 25.5% compared to the 2030 business-as-usual (BaU) scenario.

In my assessment, fossil fuel costs significantly impact the additional annual costs of the system. Depending on fuel prices, the extra annual costs range from 2.5 to 3.5 million euros. Connecting the power systems of the islands would allow for higher RES penetration—up to 42.3%—but comes at a higher annual cost of approximately 2 million euros for an extra 10 percentage points in RES share. Isolated power systems, however, achieve a 32% RES penetration with 57% lower additional costs.

From an environmental perspective, I support connecting the islands’ power systems to maximize RES penetration. Economically, I favor implementing RES in isolated systems due to lower costs. To justify the connection, I believe the islands’ power demand must increase through population growth or industrial development. I also think connecting the islands would enhance social cohesion and should be encouraged.

Finally, I suggest measures that could lead to eliminating fossil fuels entirely in both islands in the long term, serving as a starting point toward a 100% RES energy system for Pico, Faial, and the entire Azores archipelago.

   Statement: The future energy scenarios for islands should prioritize increasing the share of renewable energy sources (RES) in the total primary energy supply of the energy system. This focus extends beyond the electricity sector to the entire system, aiming to reduce reliance on fossil fuels and limit biomass use to sustainable levels. These measures are aligned with the EU's climate targets and the goal of reducing CO2 emissions. While cost reduction is a secondary consideration, it remains an important objective alongside minimizing energy losses across the system.

Islands face unique challenges, such as limited transmission lines and higher costs for imported fuels and products. To address these, future energy systems should aim to reduce imports and dependency on external resources. Instead, local resources should be utilized to the greatest sustainable extent, including repurposing otherwise exported or curtailed electricity within the local grid. Achieving this requires the integration and balancing of energy sectors to enhance efficiency and self-sufficiency.

243. ID: 6903
   Year: 2018
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Researchers
   Statement: We believe that, given the ongoing rise in sea levels and the increasing population in coastal areas, it is essential to explore more sustainable ways of utilizing the ocean for energy, food, work, and living. Our study presents the results of a model test for a floating mega island, which is designed to withstand large waves up to 15.5 meters in significant wave height. This test examines the motion response and load effects on the island, and the findings will help advance further development of these floating islands. 

The proposed island consists of 87 large floating triangular modules, which are interconnected to form a flexible floating structure with dimensions of 1.5 by 2 km, scaled at 1:250. The tests measured the island's motion response as well as the forces between the triangular modules and the mooring loads. These results, gathered using force transducers and motion sensors, demonstrate that the flexible design allows the island to move with the waves. This flexibility results in significantly reduced green water compared to rigid island structures. Our approach, similar to techniques used in offshore oil and gas operations, demonstrates the potential for innovation in large-scale ocean-based solutions.

255. ID: 3110
   Year: 2019
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Li Yang, Piman Sun
   Statement: A distributed power supply system differs from traditional centralized power systems by situating power generation equipment close to users at a small scale (ranging from a few kilowatts to 50 MW small modular systems). This decentralized system can independently supply power, heat, and cooling energy and utilizes technologies such as internal combustion engines, gas or liquid fuels, micro gas turbines, and various fuel cells. Distributed generation systems offer significant environmental benefits.

Distributed power systems have several advantages over centralized power stations:
- They eliminate the need for constructing large-scale power plants and reduce transmission and distribution costs.
- They experience minimal or no transmission and distribution losses.
- They allow flexible thermoelectric ratio adjustments.
- Their installation and construction costs are lower.
- They reduce the risk of widespread power failures since each power supply system operates independently.
- They facilitate convenient control and quality monitoring of regional power performance.
- They are ideal for providing power to rural areas, mountainous regions, development zones, residential areas, and commercial zones.

The "Energy Island," also known as Combined Cooling, Heating, and Power (CCHP), exemplifies a distributed power supply mode. It integrates heating, water heating, refrigeration, and power generation processes into a single system. The "Energy Island" significantly enhances energy efficiency, achieving an energy utilization rate of up to 90%, compared to the 30%-50% efficiency typical of ordinary power plants. This system also avoids transmission losses and reduces harmful emissions, making it a highly efficient and environmentally friendly solution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

256. ID: 2281
   Year: 2019
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Klinge Jacobsen, Henrik,  Hevia Koch, Pablo Alejandro, Christoph
   Statement: Nearshore wind development has been promoted as a cost-reducing alternative to close the gap between onshore and offshore wind projects. The cost benefits of nearshore development are linked to shallower waters, shorter distances to shore, and the potential to avoid the need for an offshore substation. Public tendering for offshore wind in Denmark has introduced nearshore wind farms as an alternative for reducing costs. However, the cost difference between nearshore and further offshore wind farms remains uncertain, as tender results have shown comparable bid levels for both locations. The main cost factor is water depth, which in Denmark often increases slowly or is unrelated to the distance from shore. Preferences for locating wind farms further offshore may be high enough to offset the increased costs. Cost and willingness-to-pay analyses need to be conducted on a case-by-case basis, considering specific cost factors and the preferences of the affected population.

263. ID: 6590
   Year: 2019
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Y. Li et al.
   Statement: Our position is that while prior research has achieved some results, it has not sufficiently addressed the interaction between VSC DC grids and renewable energy systems. Specifically, existing studies lack an in-depth focus on fault ride-through strategies and coordinated control technologies for systems integrating VSC DC grids with renewable energy. Current research primarily examines fault ride-through in cases of AC grid short-circuits or peer-to-peer VSC DC systems, neglecting the impact of VSC DC grid faults on renewable energy grid connections. 

We acknowledge that existing methods can manage DC voltage rises and provide some fault ride-through capability for renewable energy and DC grids. However, these methods inevitably affect renewable energy generators and potentially challenge the regulatory standards for their connection to DC grids. Therefore, to ensure the safety and protection of renewable energy systems, it is critical to develop fault ride-through methods that consider AC grid failures in the context of VSC DC transmission.

The project will cost between 200-300 billion Danish kroner (approximately 27-40 billion euros) and will be operational before 2030.

The surrounding wind farms will have a combined peak capacity of 10 gigawatts - equivalent to about 1,000 of today's most powerful offshore wind turbines and far exceeding the current largest offshore plant of 1.2 gigawatts. The generated electricity will be enough to power 10 million households, which is more than Denmark's entire population. The power will be transmitted to the artificial island via underwater cables and converted into storable energy forms like hydrogen, synthetic fuels, or gas using Power-to-X technologies.

The site selection and approval process should be completed by 2021, followed by construction. While there are significant technical challenges for such a large offshore project, and Power-to-X technology is currently expensive, the massive scale of these planned facilities should lead to dramatic cost reductions.

This energy island is central to Denmark's climate strategy. Under the new Climate Act passed by our Social Democratic government coalition, Denmark must cut greenhouse gas emissions by 70% by 2030, aiming for complete climate neutrality by 2050. Denmark's power grid will run on 100% renewable energy by 2028.

287. ID: 4016
   Year: 2019
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Martin Skov Skjøth-Rasmussen
   Statement: At Haldor Topsøe, we are working on a completely different approach to energy storage than the commonly discussed batteries. We focus on storing energy in chemicals such as hydrogen, methane, methanol, and ammonia, which can be used as fuel. This is where our expertise in electrolysis comes into play.

Electrolysis allows us to use excess electricity from wind turbines or solar panels to split water vapor (H2O) into oxygen and hydrogen in an electrolyzer. The hydrogen we produce can then be used for various purposes, including the production of ammonia (NH3) or upgrading biogas to natural gas (methane, CH4) by reacting the CO2 in the biogas with the hydrogen.

This process effectively stores the electrical energy as chemical energy, which can later be used as fuel for heavy transport, such as trucks and ships. In Denmark, I see enormous potential in upgrading biogas to natural gas, as we already have an extensive natural gas network and significant biogas resources, largely due to our substantial agricultural production.

Biogas contains about 30-40 percent CO2, and by upgrading it to natural gas, we can save considerable amounts of CO2 while also utilizing the CO2 as energy. In the long term, the biogas resources we have in Denmark could nearly replace the natural gas we currently extract from the North Sea. This represents a major step forward in reducing CO2 emissions and optimizing the use of our renewable energy resources.

306. ID: 981
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Rahman Daiyan, Iain MacGill and Rose Amal
   Statement: Despite the technical and, in some cases, niche commercial maturity of key technologies and some early on-ground deployment, we acknowledge that most renewable P2X products are still costlier compared to their conventional fossil-fuel-based production processes. This price variation likely arises due to the decentralized modes of P2X plants, with most P2X plants being small-scale, whereas traditional chemical and energy industries benefit from economies of scale and the ability to negotiate lower feedstock pricing. In addition, we recognize that most P2X technologies suffer from relatively high capital costs, which are projected to decline as manufacturers ramp up their production capacity, and they have large electricity requirements. There is growing consensus that the cost-competitiveness of P2X is heavily influenced by the availability of cheap and excess renewable electricity. That said, we remain optimistic about the evolving economics of these P2X technologies, which are promising and highlight the opportunity for commercial viability and scale-up. These economics are expected to improve further due to advances in catalyst and system development for both electrolysis and secondary conversion reactor systems across various P2X pathways.

In addition to capital costs and electricity pricing, we also believe that the costs of feedstock will play a crucial role in determining the price of P2X products. In particular, for several secondary conversion processes, renewable power-to-hydrogen and its associated economics will be pivotal for their feasibility.

In the following sections, we will present the outlook and challenges of different P2X technologies and discuss pathways for cost reductions.

Power-to-H2: While renewable hydrogen pricing is currently at least two times more expensive than hydrogen produced from fossil fuels, we see that declining electrolyzer capital costs, resulting from economies of scale, and the adoption of a new generation of cost-effective catalysts (either replacing commercial Pt/Ir catalysts or reducing their loading), alongside decreasing electricity prices, are driving competitive levelized costs across various jurisdictions. Although most research and demonstrations on renewable H2 have focused on using clean water, we also believe it is crucial to explore the use of wastewater and seawater as feedstock, especially in regions like Australia, North America, the Middle East, and China, where fresh water is scarce. The direct use of seawater presents challenges, such as electrode and membrane stability issues (due to impurities in seawater) and the formation of Cl2 instead of O2 during the anode reaction. Considerable research and funding are being directed toward developing stable systems that can directly use seawater or combine reverse osmosis water purification with electrolysis. In contrast, the use of wastewater for electrolysis is more mature, with a number of commercial systems capable of converting gray water to hydrogen. We expect that further research into the chemistry of these technologies will provide solutions to address water-related concerns in hydrogen production.

328. ID: 689
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: Q: Can the minister confirm that the potential for the so-called Power-to-X (PtX) products and energy storage is relatively limited before 2030? If so, could the minister explain what this means for the profitability of the project regarding the establishment of an "energy island"?

A: Regarding the establishment of one or more potential energy islands, the spread of PtX production could lead to synergies due to a more efficient utilization of the island's offshore wind production. This is partly because hydrogen production via electrolysis can consume electricity more flexibly and intermittently than other types of consumption. Thus, electrolysis can occur when offshore wind electricity is abundant and cheap, and conversely, it can be disconnected during shortages. If a flexible electrolysis plant is integrated with an energy island and placed in the same location on the grid as the island’s offshore wind production, the need for extensive upgrades to the transmission grid could be reduced, as the plant could act as a "buffer" between large-scale RE electricity production and the grid.

The use of PtX production in conjunction with an energy island could thus raise the threshold for how much RE can be efficiently integrated into Denmark’s energy system. The larger the capacity of flexible PtX production placed in the same location on the grid as the island’s offshore wind production, the more offshore wind capacity can be connected to and landed from the island, thereby increasing the value of offshore wind production, relieving the electricity transmission grid, and reducing the need for internal grid upgrades. Therefore, we must consider the possibility of developing potential energy islands in phases as Denmark also scales up and potentially accelerates PtX production and demand.

330. ID: 687
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: Kraka’s report also discusses long-term electricity prices and project economics. Here, I would like to note that there is inherent uncertainty about the future—especially for a project of the size and duration of the North Sea Energy Island. This uncertainty particularly applies to electricity price projections. However, uncertainty is not an argument against making decisions, which I note Kraka also acknowledges in its report. Instead, we strive to mitigate risks continuously. One way is to diversify risks by, for example, allowing room for innovation and expanding the island's portfolio, such as supporting the production and distribution of hydrogen or other green gases from the island, or supporting other large-scale consumers like data centers.

Another way to spread risk is through the choice of ownership model. In the agreement, we decided that the project would be based on shared ownership, with the state owning 50.1% of the island and a private partner owning 49.9%. The private co-owner will be selected through a competitive tender process. Shared ownership has the advantage that the island's economics are market-tested, and the risk is shared, as both parties bear the subsequent financial responsibilities of the project.

340. ID: 7071
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Alessandro Singlitico, Nicolas Jean Bernard Campion, Marie Münster, Matti Juhani Koivisto, Nicolaos Antonio Cutululis, Cathy Jingqing Suo, Kenneth Karlsson, Torben Jørgensen, Jeppe Eimose Waagstein, Maja F. Bendtsen
   Statement: Bornholm has the potential to become the first natural energy hub in the Baltic Sea due to its strategic position for offshore wind power expansion, planned energy interconnections, and the need for storing and converting surplus power. Bornholm could serve as both a center for electrical equipment, including substations and connection nodes between countries, and a hub for power-to-x (P2X) production using offshore wind power.

A preliminary investigation shows that placing an electrolyser in Bornholm would result in lower hydrogen production costs than placing it in Copenhagen. However, Bornholm faces limitations, including restricted access to carbon dioxide (CO2), oxygen (O2), and heat consumers. The CO2 available from combined heat and power (CHP) plants burning biomass and biogas production from all digestible wet feedstocks would be insufficient to meet Rønne Havn's demand for renewable fuels.

To achieve immediate decarbonization of the maritime transport sector, converting hydrogen into a drop-in fuel is necessary, with methanol being the most promising alternative. However, the CO2 available from biomass combustion and biogas production is insufficient to meet the methanol demand of ferries, covering only about half of the requirement.

The lowest methanol production cost, calculated at €589 per tonne, occurs when the electrolyser is located on Bornholm, has access to the public grid, faces no CO2 limitations, and all by-products (heat and oxygen) are sold. Conversely, placing an electrolyser in Copenhagen would result in higher hydrogen production costs due to elevated grid connection expenses and the higher cost of electricity delivered onshore from offshore wind power plants (OWPP). 

For optimal cost efficiency, a large share of the electricity consumed by the electrolyser would need to come from the public grid, as the price of grid electricity is often lower than the cost of delivering offshore wind power onshore. However, due to Bornholm's resource limitations, Copenhagen could become a more favorable location if CO2 is available in sufficient quantities and all by-products can be sold without restrictions.

Producing hydrogen offshore without the ability to sell by-products is the most expensive option. Increasing system flexibility would significantly improve the economic potential of offshore electrolysers.

343. ID: 2827
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: Job creation and innovation
   Actor: Jakob Nørmark
   Statement: As Bornholms Tidende, I can tell you that the construction of offshore wind farms connected to an energy island/hub is possible in all the investigated areas, including 10 gigawatts in the three areas in the North Sea and 3 gigawatts in Bornholm I+II. The screening found a total capacity of 18 gigawatts. However, for the areas in the Baltic Sea, it is recommended that a more detailed analysis of the sensitivity of selected bird species be conducted, and consideration should be given to cables, pipelines, and existing shipping routes.

The cost of constructing offshore wind farms near Bornholm with a total capacity of 3 gigawatts is estimated at 58.26 billion Danish kroner. This is approximately 370 million kroner cheaper than the calculated investments for 3 gigawatts in the North Sea energy island project, with a price difference of less than 1%. Utilizing Bornholm's solid ground avoids the 3.6 billion kroner expense for establishing an energy island, which is only included in the North Sea calculation. However, the expenses for new export cables to Zealand and Poland for Bornholm are valued at 23.7 billion kroner, which is 6.7 billion kroner more than the cable expenses in the North Sea.

The long-term expenses relative to the amount of electricity produced indicate that it appears to be more cost-effective to invest in the North Sea. The North Sea project is more efficient than the Bornholm project due to a better wind resource and cheaper export connections. The wind blows at 10.73 meters per second in the North Sea, while it averages 9.92 meters per second south of Bornholm.

The western part of Bornholm II is located in an internationally important bird area, where long-tailed ducks, velvet scoters, and common scoters overwinter. There is a risk that these species will be displaced from an important foraging area if offshore wind turbines are installed. Additionally, the Baltic Sea area between Denmark, Sweden, and Germany is important for crane and raptor migration. Bornholm I and II lie in the migration routes for birds that breed in Sweden and Norway and overwinter to the south.

The seabed in the two Bornholm fields is rated as "less suitable" compared to the North Sea areas. The area is considered less suitable for foundation with monopiles due to the possible presence of hard clay with stones, high-lying hard and flint-rich chalk, and high-lying, possibly cemented marine deposits. However, no geological or geotechnical factors have been found that would prevent the placement of offshore wind turbine foundations.

The two Danish power grids have limited capacity. Due to the capacity ceiling, it is assumed that only 1 gigawatt produced at Bornholm will go to the Danish grid, while the remaining 1-2 gigawatts will be sent abroad, likely through the proposed connection to Poland.

In the wind turbines, alternating current is produced with a voltage of 66 kilovolts. Transformer platforms will be built at sea near the wind turbines, where the voltage will be raised to 220 kilovolts. From there, parallel cable systems, each with a total installed capacity of 500 megawatts, will be built. If 2 gigawatts are installed, four export cables must be brought ashore, where a transformer station near the coast converts the alternating current to direct current.

An area just north of Hasle has been designated as the location where the power will be brought ashore. Energinet has identified an area of 4-6 hectares where there is room for the facility. However, the location of the onshore facility could be moved along the coast, depending on the preliminary project.

Finally, our vision includes a climate-neutral waste sector by 2030, with a significant reduction in the burning of plastic and an increase in recycling. This will contribute to the overall reduction in Denmark's carbon footprint.

The Ministry of Finance will ensure that these ambitious measures are financially supported, contributing to Denmark's goal of a sustainable, low-carbon economy.

349. ID: 168

   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: I, on behalf of the Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities, outlines the vision and strategic priorities for the energy island concept. An energy island is designed to serve as a hub for offshore wind energy production, enabling efficient use of offshore wind potential far from the coast while integrating significantly more renewable energy into the European energy system—a critical step for the green transition. The island will connect nearby offshore wind farms, distributing electricity directly to multiple countries via export cables, which also reduce the need for onshore infrastructure investments by serving as both landing and trading cables. This dual functionality can lead to significant cost savings and minimizes the need for expanding Denmark's onshore grid.

However, realizing these benefits requires addressing challenges such as the historically long development times for export connections, which can take 8–9 years. Political agreements with relevant neighboring countries need to be finalized promptly to ensure the energy island project can be completed by 2030. To support this initiative, 65 million DKK was allocated in the 2020 Finance Act for preliminary investigations, including 26 million DKK for fine-screening suitable locations based on environmental, natural, and planning factors. These analyses will also evaluate the economic feasibility of the project and the role of export connections in ensuring profitability.

In parallel, the Ministry has initiated informal dialogues with North Sea countries to explore collaborative opportunities, further ensuring that the energy island project is positioned as a cornerstone for both Denmark's and Europe's renewable energy future.

As end-users, we are focused on identifying the modifications required for our ships to use electrofuels and the necessary adjustments across the bunkering system and supply chain to facilitate the transition.

Even with a fully operational 1.3 GW plant, the facility would supply only a small fraction of our fleet's needs. Scaling this effort globally for the entire shipping industry would require approximately 1,000 plants of this size. Despite this, we see the Copenhagen project as a critical starting point, helping to kickstart electrofuel production in Denmark and potentially positioning Denmark as a global leader in this field. Denmark's strengths in wind energy and advanced Power-to-X technologies make it uniquely positioned to lead this transition.

However, significant investments will be required to retrofit ships and adapt supply chains. The greater challenge lies in developing these new fuels and building the infrastructure to produce them. To overcome this, we need incentives, such as a carbon tax on fossil fuels, to offset the higher cost of green fuels. Additionally, Mærsk is working to reduce fuel consumption and improve efficiency, aiming to cut CO2 emissions per container transported by 60% by 2030 compared to 2008 levels."

398. ID: 4692
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Totalförsvarets forskningsinstitut (FOI)
   Statement: The Swedish climate goal for 2040 is to exclusively produce renewable electricity. This readjustment has resulted in a dramatic increase in the number of solar power producers, an increase which is expected to continue in the coming years. Concurrently however, this rapid growth has also raised the concern of radio frequency interference in the proximity of such photovoltaic systems. During last year, a number of interference incidents were reported. Though problems have mainly been observed at frequencies pertaining to the high frequency (HF) band, interference has also been noticed in even higher frequency bands which are used by cellular systems and communications for rescue services and police. The objective of this report is to give an overview of the interference emitted from photovoltaic systems that has been reported on in Sweden as well as in other countries. The report also provides an overview of the scientific research on the topic of electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) and photovoltaic systems, which has been studied under many years. Of great interest is also the measurement campaigns which has been conducted on interference generated by photovoltaic systems. Considering the observed radio interference and the recently published scientific reports on the subject, there is no doubt in the existence of interference caused by photovoltaic systems. However, how frequently such interference occurs and how strong the interference level is for different types of systems, remain unanswered questions. Nevertheless, if the issue of radio interference is not addressed, the ever increasing number of photovoltaic systems risk to inherently lead to more interference incidents.

437. ID: 1844
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: COWI
   Statement: The western part of Bornholm II is located in an internationally important bird area. The area is a wintering ground for long-tailed ducks, velvet scoters, and common scoters, which feed on blue mussels that are abundant in the region. We think that in this part of Bornholm II, there is a risk that these species could be displaced from an important feeding area if offshore wind turbines are installed. The area is a so-called IBA (Important Bird Area) designated by the international organization BirdLife International. However, it is not covered by international directives or conventions such as Natura 2000. We recommend conducting a detailed analysis of the sensitivity of these bird species.

Additionally, the Baltic Sea area between Denmark, Sweden, and Germany is important for crane and raptor migration. Bornholm I and II are located along the migratory routes of birds that breed in Sweden and Norway and winter further south. We think there is a risk that the installation of offshore wind turbines could create a barrier effect or pose a collision risk for migrating birds, which also calls for a more comprehensive analysis of migratory birds.

452. ID: 3859
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Mr. Ernst van Zuijlen
   Statement: The IJVER energy island project aims to construct an artificial pilot island in the Ijmuiden Ver area designated for wind farms. This energy island will be multifunctional, incorporating electrical infrastructure such as an HVDC station and interconnections, a hydrogen production facility connected to the existing gas grid, and facilities for the operation and maintenance of nearby wind farms. Additional uses include aquaculture, fisheries, and marine research.

The business case relies on the island's energy-related functions, including serving as an offshore grid hub, producing hydrogen, and supporting operation and maintenance activities. The design considers various concepts, such as rock revetments, caisson protection, artificial reefs, and even the innovative Hybrid Enersea Hub, which uses floating elements with breakwaters to adapt to metocean conditions.

The hydrogen production facility includes components like water purification, alkaline electrolysis, compression, and storage. As a pilot project, further research and development will optimize individual components and the system as a whole. The project also explores ecological synergies, tidal properties, morphology, and legal challenges, such as international law, ownership, and regulatory frameworks.

453. ID: 7010
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Alessandro Singlitico, Nicolas Jean Bernard Campion, Marie Münster, Matti Juhani Koivisto, Nicolaos Antonio Cutululis, Cathy Jingqing Suo, Kenneth Karlsson, Torben Jørgensen, Jeppe Eimose Waagstein, Maja F. Bendtsen
   Statement: Bornholm has the potential to become the first natural energy hub in the Baltic Sea due to its strategic position for offshore wind power expansion, planned energy interconnections, and the need for storing and converting surplus power. Bornholm could serve as both a center for electrical equipment, including substations and connection nodes between countries, and a hub for power-to-x (P2X) production using offshore wind power.
A preliminary investigation shows that placing an electrolyser in Bornholm would result in lower hydrogen production costs than placing it in Copenhagen. However, Bornholm faces limitations, including restricted access to carbon dioxide (CO2), oxygen (O2), and heat consumers. The CO2 available from combined heat and power (CHP) plants burning biomass and biogas production from all digestible wet feedstocks would be insufficient to meet Rønne Havn's demand for renewable fuels.
To achieve immediate decarbonization of the maritime transport sector, converting hydrogen into a drop-in fuel is necessary, with methanol being the most promising alternative. However, the CO2 available from biomass combustion and biogas production is insufficient to meet the methanol demand of ferries, covering only about half of the requirement.
The lowest methanol production cost, calculated at €589 per tonne, occurs when the electrolyser is located on Bornholm, has access to the public grid, faces no CO2 limitations, and all by-products (heat and oxygen) are sold. Conversely, placing an electrolyser in Copenhagen would result in higher hydrogen production costs due to elevated grid connection expenses and the higher cost of electricity delivered onshore from offshore wind power plants (OWPP). 
For optimal cost efficiency, a large share of the electricity consumed by the electrolyser would need to come from the public grid, as the price of grid electricity is often lower than the cost of delivering offshore wind power onshore. However, due to Bornholm's resource limitations, Copenhagen could become a more favorable location if CO2 is available in sufficient quantities and all by-products can be sold without restrictions.
Producing hydrogen offshore without the ability to sell by-products is the most expensive option. Increasing system flexibility would significantly improve the economic potential of offshore electrolysers.

457. ID: 5571
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: I cannot support lifting the state's area reservations for the Bornholm local wind project at this time. We are in the middle of planning a massive expansion of offshore wind through state tenders, following both the 2018 Energy Agreement and the 2020 Climate Agreement for Energy and Industry. We have initiated a new era for offshore wind with energy islands in Denmark, including the decision to advance the Hesselø Offshore Wind Farm (800-1,200 MW) and two energy islands - one in the North Sea and one on Bornholm - with a total of 5 GW connected initially, and the potential for 10 GW in the North Sea later.

The Bornholm energy island project alone will generate 2 GW by 2030, producing more electricity than Bornholm's entire annual consumption. Profitability of these energy islands depends on securing adequate sales opportunities for the green electricity produced. Given these massive state-planned expansions, it would be inappropriate to lift the state's area reservations now.

Regarding local ownership, I cannot support increasing the buyer's rights scheme from 20% to 50% local ownership. The Justice Ministry previously found that even a 33.3% mandatory local ownership would violate EU's right of establishment and make Denmark less attractive for wind development. Moreover, we have actually terminated the buyer's rights scheme as of June 1, 2020, as analysis showed it failed to increase local acceptance of wind projects. We have replaced it with a RE-bonus and a green pool system.

I also cannot support providing state guarantees for project development under the open-door scheme, as this would mean the state taking on unlimited risk without project control. The state should only bear development risks for projects it initiates through tenders.

459. ID: 3863
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Klemens Kaar
   Statement: Renewable hydrogen has the potential to decarbonize sectors that are difficult to electrify and are currently not being addressed. Without integrating flexible solutions like direct electrification or additional supply, significant amounts of electricity from renewable energy sources would go to waste. Electrolysers are ideal for flexible consumption because they can quickly adapt to fluctuating renewable energy production, absorb large amounts of electricity, and convert it into hydrogen, enabling long-term storage compared to batteries.   When wind resources exceed the capacity of transmission to demand centers, electrolysis can convert excess wind energy into hydrogen, adding economic value to high production periods. This approach facilitates the expansion of wind energy capacity alongside electrolysis, which could reach 450GW in Europe according to recent studies. An example is the Westküste100 or Hydrogen Region West Coast project, which integrates offshore and onshore wind power with local industrial hydrogen demands and on-site storage. The project takes a holistic approach, spanning renewable power production, fuel production and distribution, and end-use in industries and aviation.  The joint venture involves ten partners and is progressing from operating a 30MW electrolysis system with storage and infrastructure to building a >100MW pilot plant for applications in refineries, mobility, and gas grids. The ultimate goal is scaling up to a ~700MW electrolysis system for green hydrogen and e-fuels across multiple sectors. To achieve this, legal uncertainties must be resolved. A favorable regulatory framework is essential, incentivizing hydrogen demand while mandating the production of hydrogen from renewable power and exempting it from the German EEG2 renewables levy, as outlined in the German national hydrogen strategy.

Six archaeologists will further explore and investigate these sites to uncover more traces from the past.

492. ID: 2114
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Society for Nature Conservation
   Statement: Danmarks Naturfredningsforening states: "The creation of new hard-bottom elements, such as the structures from turbine foundations and the outer components of the energy island, will attract sessile species and potentially other species not typically found in sandy seabed areas. However, this does not inherently increase biodiversity, nor should it automatically be considered beneficial. The sandy seabed being replaced is a natural habitat type that, while having a lower biodiversity compared to a stone reef, is highly productive and rich in small mussels and bristle worms that are critical as a food source for fish. The conversion from sandy seabed to reef-like structures is not a biodiversity improvement but rather a total alteration of the habitat type. While the new structures may attract species associated with stone reefs, they can also facilitate the spread of invasive species to areas where they do not naturally occur. Additionally, this change represents a shift from one natural biotope to another, artificially created one—a transformation that would not typically be permitted on land."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bornholm is ideal because it already exists and provides the infrastructure and accessibility necessary to start testing quickly. The island’s compact size, existing societal structures, and ease of navigation make it a practical and efficient testing ground. In contrast, the North Sea energy island will pose significant logistical challenges, including helicopter transport, access clearance, and harsh weather conditions.  

Bornholm offers the opportunity to experiment with various configurations and control methods in a flexible environment accustomed to functioning as a living energy laboratory. Once these solutions are tested and proven on Bornholm, they can be replicated on the North Sea energy island and other future energy islands in Denmark and internationally.  

The foundation is in place, and there is no reason to delay. Initial testing and installations can begin immediately to accelerate innovation at the pace necessary for the energy islands to support the urgent green transition.

496. ID: 2109
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Society for Nature Conservation
   Statement: We are deeply concerned about the impact of the Bornholm Energy Island construction on the critically endangered Baltic Sea porpoise population. The specific area designated for offshore wind turbines serves as winter habitat for these porpoises. The total population consists of only 500 individuals, with fewer than 100 being breeding females. According to an ICES report, the loss of even one individual per year from human activities like bycatch could have devastating effects on the entire population. Since Baltic Sea porpoises are protected under Annex IV, Denmark has a legal obligation to protect these marine mammals wherever they are found.

The environmental impact assessment for Bornholm Energy Island must thoroughly address and detail specific measures to protect the porpoise population from underwater noise pollution, both during the construction phase and the operational phase of the wind turbines.

516. ID: 1850
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Mogens Lykketoft
   Statement: We must build these energy islands to help meet the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit. The North Sea has the potential to generate more energy than all the oil and gas Denmark has ever produced there. Building artificial islands is the most efficient and cost-effective way to connect and distribute massive amounts of offshore wind power, not just to Denmark but to the entire European grid.

The energy islands solve multiple problems by creating a hub-and-spoke system. Instead of having scattered, individual wind farms providing small amounts of power to individual areas, these islands will serve as central collection and distribution hubs. By connecting different types of energy sources - solar, wind, hydroelectric, and nuclear - across Europe through these hubs, we can better balance the power grid without needing to store enormous amounts of wind energy.

The energy islands represent a shift from fragmented national climate policies to an integrated, transnational approach that connects multiple energy sectors. This is crucial for effectively integrating renewable energy into our power systems. However, I acknowledge that we still face significant challenges, particularly regarding energy storage solutions for these islands.

548. ID: 4346
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: A broad majority in the Danish Parliament has agreed to establish a new artificial Energy Island in the North Sea, 80 kilometers off the Danish coast, with a total estimated cost of 210 billion kroner. This project will feature offshore wind farms surrounding the island with turbines expected to reach unprecedented heights of over 260 meters. The Energy Island will collect and distribute electricity generated by these wind farms, supporting Denmark’s green transition and enabling the export of renewable energy.

Initially, the wind farms will provide three gigawatts of electricity, enough to power three million European households. Eventually, the capacity will increase to ten gigawatts, powering ten million households. The island will also support Power-to-X technology to convert offshore wind power into fuels for ships, planes, and trucks. The island, when fully built, will cover an area equivalent to 64 football fields.

Despite criticism from Ørsted, which raised concerns about the cost, inflexibility, and feasibility of producing hydrogen on the island, the project will proceed as planned. The state will retain majority ownership to ensure the infrastructure remains under national control, making this the largest public-private partnership in Denmark’s history. The investor consortium Vindø, which includes PensionDanmark and Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, has shown interest in the project.

This Energy Island is a cornerstone of Denmark’s 70% CO2 reduction goal by 2030 and represents a key initiative to position Denmark as a global leader in renewable energy. The North Sea project follows a separate agreement to establish a two-gigawatt Energy Island in the Baltic Sea, where Bornholm will serve as the hub for offshore wind power.

571. ID: 2102
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Society for Nature Conservation
   Statement: We are deeply concerned about placing the new Bornholm I and II wind farm areas on either side of the protected marine area 'Adler Grund and Rønne Banke'. This area is designated as Natura 2000 and is critical habitat for the highly endangered Baltic Sea porpoise population. The area was also recently designated as a bird protection area under this year's Habitat Order.

Danmarks Naturfredningsforening insists on an extremely thorough investigation of how building offshore wind farms in this pristine area, directly adjacent to a protected zone, will impact the species protected under Natura 2000. The environmental assessment of the marine plan indicates there is a risk of permanent displacement of seabirds, including long-tailed ducks, common scoters, and velvet scoters. Any such displacement would violate the Habitats Directive.

Building wind farms in these locations, where none currently exist and right next to a protected area, requires the utmost scrutiny to ensure compliance with environmental protection laws and prevent harm to endangered species.

The project, estimated to cost 280 billion Danish kroner, has been in discussion for several years and has now been approved by a majority in the Danish Parliament.

The state-owned energy company Energinet outlines that the island will span at least 120,000 square meters, an area equivalent to 18 football fields. The island, called an “energy island,” will act as a power hub, receiving electricity from hundreds of offshore wind turbines. Initially, it will host 200 wind turbines with a total capacity of three gigawatts, with plans to expand to ten gigawatts in the future. This increase in capacity is projected to meet the energy needs of up to ten million households. 

Additionally, the energy produced by the island will also support transportation and heavy traffic, including trucks and buses.

586. ID: 3047
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Hans Østergård
   Statement: The two mayors, Hans Østergård from Ringkøbing Skjern Municipality and Erik Flyvholm from Lemvig Municipality, see no reason for the establishment of the two near-shore offshore wind farms. Their reasoning is as follows:

1) Currently, Denmark has so much wind energy that many onshore wind turbines must be throttled down. The energy cannot yet be stored for use during calm periods or converted into other forms of energy.
2) The Thor offshore wind farm, with a capacity of 800-1000 MW, located about 20 km from the coast near Thorsminde, is expected to be completed by 2025/2026. Additionally, the Kriegers Flak project in the Baltic Sea, with a capacity of 600 MW, is being phased in. This will bring the total offshore wind capacity from 1700 MW in 2021 to around 2300 MW. By 2025/2026, the Thor project will increase the total to 3300 MW, almost doubling the current capacity. Therefore, the two near-shore wind farms, with a total capacity of 350 MW, are unnecessary and will only cause even more onshore turbines to stand still due to a lack of demand for electricity.
3) By 2025/2026, the mayors hope that Power-to-X technology will be developed, along with the necessary number of electric vehicle charging stations and the conversion of electricity into liquid fuel.
4) Cancelling the near-shore wind farms would save the state millions of kroner, even after compensating Vattenfall. Additionally, the fishing industries from Hvide Sande, Thorsminde, and Thyborøn would benefit from better and freer fishing conditions in the waters 0-20 km off the coast from Hvide Sande to Thyborøn.
5) The mayors are optimistic that the Energy Island in the waters off their municipalities will create many service-related jobs, and they are ready to engage in discussions to make this a win-win situation.

They look forward to hearing from Energy Minister Dan Jørgensen to arrange further discussions.

For my thesis, I chose to focus on Denmark's energy policy, particularly the interplay of interests within the energy sector. During this research, I discovered that Denmark does not actually get 50% of its energy from clean sources, as is often claimed. In reality, back then it was only about 8%, and today it’s closer to 9%. I felt compelled to highlight this fact, as it is rarely addressed in public debates.
I’ve also done some calculations regarding the energy island’s output over its lifetime. It’s expected to generate enough electricity to cover Denmark’s electricity consumption for 30 years. However, if the same amount of money were invested in building a standard nuclear power plant, we could generate enough electricity to cover our needs for 114 years. In addition, we would have free district heating to cover all our heating requirements for those same 114 years.
We often hear that this energy island will deliver 10 GW, but that’s its capacity. The wind doesn’t blow all the time, so the actual output will only be about 4.5 GW when adjusted for intermittency. For the same investment, you could instead have built 7 GW of nuclear power, which produces a steady output consistently.
