1348. ID: 162
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Climate, Energy and Utilities Committee
   Statement: I have approved Energinet’s application for the "Energy Island Bornholm electrical infrastructure" project. The project involves establishing a 245 km direct current connection between Bornholm and Zealand, along with two 400 kV stations with converter facilities on Bornholm and Zealand. This infrastructure will connect Energy Island Bornholm to Denmark's electricity transmission grid.  

Following a political supplementary agreement on August 29, 2022, the Energy Island Bornholm project has been expanded from 2 GW to 3 GW. Additionally, a political agreement with Germany was reached on July 26, 2022, enabling Germany to connect to Energy Island Bornholm. Energinet has preliminarily assessed that this agreement will reduce the project’s budget due to cost-sharing with the German TSO, 50Hertz. As a result, Energinet’s construction budget has been reduced from 16.9 billion DKK to approximately 13.9 billion DKK, excluding risk costs. Similarly, annual operating costs have been reduced from 121 million DKK to 114 million DKK.  

Energinet’s application has been reviewed based on the submitted materials, including the technical solutions and assumptions outlined in the business case. The project must proceed in accordance with these specifications. Any significant changes to the project must be promptly reported to the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities for separate approval.

1376. ID: 4845
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Claus Møller
   Statement: The enthusiasm surrounding Power-to-X (PtX) and its role in the green transition is evident, with numerous seminars and large-scale plans being discussed across Europe. The EU is even offering significant financial incentives, including €750 billion in COVID-recovery funds, to support PtX plants and hydrogen infrastructure like pipelines and storage.  

However, the conversation often overlooks the poor efficiency of the conversion from electricity to hydrogen, which, with current technologies, struggles to exceed 50%. One suggested solution is to use the excess heat for district heating, but this raises serious practical concerns.  

Take Esbjerg as an example. When the Esbjerg plant—a 378 MW facility that supplied electricity and heat—closes in 2023, its heating will be replaced with a combination of a 50 MW seawater heat pump, a 60 MW biomass plant, and a 30 MW electric boiler. Yet, plans for energy conversion in Esbjerg include:  

- Høst PtX Esbjerg with 1 GW capacity  
- H2 Energy with 1 GW capacity  
- A fully built-out hydrogen factory at 12 MW  
- Various pyrolysis plants exceeding 10 MW  

All these projects claim their waste heat can be used for district heating, but the combined output would be around 20 times the actual heating demand in Esbjerg. This mismatch highlights the inefficiency and lack of foresight in these plans.  

On a broader scale, the same inefficiency exists for energy islands in the North and Baltic Seas. Performing energy conversion at sea, where there is no need for district heating, exacerbates the issue of waste. While some envision humans colonizing Mars or the Moon, perhaps it would be more practical and cost-effective to build artificial islands in the North Sea to utilize this excess heat. Yet, even this is unlikely to be part of current plans.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1386. ID: 4795
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Cheers to this milestone! 🍾🥂

Denmark is about to gain an additional island—the world’s first energy island, to be established 80 km off the coast in the North Sea.

The energy island will be constructed as an artificial island designed to collect and distribute electricity from surrounding offshore wind farms. Initially, the island will have a capacity of 3 GW, enough to power 3 million European households. Over time, the capacity will be expanded to 10 GW 😵

While the exact design is still being finalized, the island, capable of handling 3 gigawatts of offshore wind power, is expected to cover at least 120,000 m², which is equivalent to 18 football fields 🤘

Eventually, the capacity will be increased from 3 to 10 gigawatts, enough to power 10 million households. When expanded, the island is expected to occupy a minimum area equivalent to 64 football fields.

Upon completion of the first phase, Denmark’s offshore wind capacity will be nearly four times larger than it is today. By the time the energy islands are fully built, the installed capacity will be seven times greater than our current capacity 💪

1398. ID: 4428

   Statement: The goal of the new supplier association, Agro Energi, which we are establishing with the Central Jutland Agricultural Association, is to handle the negotiations with the companies that farmers will engage with—whether that’s in biogas, grass protein, or pyrolysis. Farmers should not have to manage these negotiations alone. We are working to establish clear and uniform framework conditions for things like pricing, raw material quality, and the allocation of climate benefits. Right now, large companies approach individual farmers to negotiate contracts, but we are determined to standardize the demands farmers make, so that we can unite in what we require.

Agro Energi is here to directly serve the individual farmer, not other associations. We will also offer legal support, ensuring that a lawyer is available to help our members if needed. But the main purpose of Agro Energi is to provide the knowledge, volume, and strength to secure the best deals, ultimately increasing and securing value-added trade in biomass and CO2 credits within agriculture.

Farmers must be credited for their biomass, and if we don't get climate credit for it, we will demand additional payment, because if we don't, we’ll have to buy credits elsewhere. Without this, we can’t meet our reduction targets. In some regions of Denmark, large energy islands are quickly emerging, opening up opportunities for new markets and business ventures, but also increasing competition and strengthening the negotiating power of companies. Agro Energi will address these challenges head-on.

I can't say for certain how much support we will have, but I strongly believe that many farmers will recognize the need to come together. Our goal is to grow to a size where we can’t be ignored, ensuring that we have the resources and financial stability to tackle this job effectively.

I am proud to say that we reached an important agreement. By 2030, we will collectively aim for a capacity of at least 19.6 gigawatts of offshore wind in the Baltic Sea—a sevenfold increase from the current 3 gigawatts. This is a major step forward for the region.

Looking further ahead, we recognize the incredible potential of offshore wind in the Baltic Sea. By 2050, the capacity could reach up to 93 gigawatts, according to estimates from the European Commission. This underlines just how critical the Baltic Sea is to our collective green transition.

I’m optimistic about what we can achieve when we work together, and this agreement is a testament to the shared commitment of the Baltic Sea nations to a greener and more secure energy future.

1441. ID: 6958
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Jens-Otto A. Sonne Risegaard
   Statement: I strongly oppose the proposed land facility for the Energy Island project on Bornholm, it would severely damage the island’s natural environment and its experience. I argue that the planned facility, consisting of three to five buildings, each 25 meters high and 100 meters long, would be impossible to hide and would significantly harm the landscape and wildlife. The facility would cover 70-90 hectares, likely be fenced off, and illuminated during the night, possibly with sensors detecting movement, which would be highly destructive to nature.
The location proposed by Energinet on South Bornholm is not a good spot, between Sose and Limensgade, as it is surrounded by roads, makes the facility visible from all directions. I suggest that an alternative location near a forest would have minimized its visibility. Additionally, the area has high groundwater levels, which could cause flooding during rainy periods, and that water drainage is primarily directed through Risebæk into the Baltic Sea.
The farmland in this area, one of the best on Bornholm, is also rich in iron oxide, which has previously caused pollution in the protected Risebæk river. Past drainage and excavation activities have contaminated the river with iron oxide, turning the water red/orange and periodically destroying all aquatic life. This pollution extends all the way to the river's outlet in the Baltic Sea, known as the "red waterfall."

1464. ID: 6881
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: COWI
   Statement: Experience that we have from other projects shows that visibility of local businesses and access to relevant suppliers are crucial for securing tasks within the local business community. It's equally important to foster relationships between contractors/operators and local companies, ensuring that tasks assigned to local businesses are completed successfully, and that quality and documentation requirements align with expectations from the outset. As an example, in the Fehmarn Belt construction, Fehmarn Belt Development created the 'Fehmarn Belt Marketplace,' a digital platform where local companies can present their services and competencies to contractors. The platform was launched alongside the first major contracts to help contractors discover local capabilities. However, it quickly became evident that large contractors preferred sourcing suppliers through their own tender portals rather than using the Marketplace. As a result, the platform was refocused to connect subcontractors with smaller local businesses for specific tasks during the construction phase. Additionally, the platform serves as a place for contractors to find solutions to unexpected needs or unforeseen tasks. Over time, the platform has developed networking activities to strengthen cooperation among local companies, increasing the likelihood of local businesses bidding for larger projects in partnerships. It also facilitates better referrals among companies when they become aware of new opportunities. The website is designed with a search function that allows users to search across industries and for specific services or competencies, so companies are encouraged to provide detailed, English-language descriptions. The platform includes a broad range of industries, from construction to services like cleaning, accounting, and transport. To be listed, companies must pay an annual membership fee, which supports the operation of the portal by Femern Belt Development. This fee has proven to be a key validation point, ensuring that only serious companies are registered on the platform.

1472. ID: 6898
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: COWI
   Statement: We believe that a fourth potential opportunity lies in positioning the Energy Island of Bornholm as a tourist attraction, blending technology, sustainability, and tourism. There are several successful examples where technology and energy have been communicated as experiences. The Østerild Wind Turbine Test Center in Thy, for instance, serves as both a knowledge hub and a tourist attraction, often visited by those who also explore the Thy National Park visitor center. Similarly, the Energy Museum in Bjerringbro showcases the history of hydropower through a functioning hydroelectric plant, attracting around 40,000 visitors annually. Universe on Als, an experience center focused on technology and science for families, welcomed 134,000 guests in 2021. Naturkraft at Ringkøbing, despite facing financial difficulties, aims to communicate nature, sustainability, and climate through its ambitious outdoor family experience center, with a goal of 280,000 visitors annually, though initial attendance has been much lower.

These examples demonstrate that while communicating nature, energy, and climate as experiences is possible, it requires the right concept and often significant investment. For Bornholm, one idea could be offering boat trips to the offshore wind turbines, allowing visitors to get a close-up view. However, this would likely require permission from the energy companies and regulatory authorities. Another possibility could involve utilizing surplus heat from the transformer station to create wellness experiences, such as hot springs. Similar to Læsø, where a spa uses salt from the island’s saltworks, Bornholm could develop hot springs powered by renewable energy, offering either wellness or health benefits to visitors.

   Statement: Energy security and the fight against climate change are crucial to the future of the European Union. Recalling the Versailles conclusions on energy, the European Commission’s communication on Joint European Action for more affordable, secure and sustainable energy, and the most recent IPCC report and taking note of the European Commission’s REPowerEU announcement of 18 May, we aim to take urgent and immediate action. The recent geopolitical events will accelerate our efforts to reduce fossil fuel consumption and promote the deployment of renewable energy for more energy resilience in Europe.
Therefore, we will increasingly replace fossil fuels, including Russian oil, coal and gas, with
European renewable energy from the North Sea, including offshore wind and green hydrogen, contributing to both EU climate neutrality and energy security. To achieve this and to pave the way for the further expansion of offshore wind, we have decided to jointly develop The North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe, an offshore renewable energy
system connecting Belgium, Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands and possibly other North Sea partners, including the members of the North Seas Energy Cooperation (NSEC). As Members of NSEC, we will build on the work already accomplished and will implement strategies to achieve our goals in close cooperation with the other regional countries and the European Commission. In doing so, we will strive for a balanced coexistence of economic and ecological needs. The North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe will consist of multiple connected offshore energy projects and hubs, offshore wind production at massive scale as well as electricity and green hydrogen interconnectors. We aim for a cost-efficient buildout of offshore wind that will harvest the potential of the North Sea in the most beneficial way for both the connected countries and the European Union overall.
Together, we have set ambitious combined targets for offshore wind of at least 65 GW by 2030. Based on the North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe, together we aim to more than double our total capacity of offshore wind to at least 150 GW by 2050, delivering more than half of capacity needed to reach EU climate neutrality according to the European Commission’s Strategy on Offshore Renewable Energy. This will contribute to large-scale onshore and offshore production of green hydrogen. We have set combined targets of about 20 GW production capacity already by 2030 and look to expand our production even further for 2050.

The environmental assessment process is a crucial step towards realizing the North Sea Energy Island, which will significantly impact the transition away from fossil fuels in both Denmark and Europe. The project aims to produce energy from offshore wind on an unprecedented scale. 

Given the innovative nature of this project, public input is vital. We strongly encourage individuals with an interest in the North Sea Energy Island to provide feedback, ask questions, and suggest topics they would like addressed in the strategic environmental assessment, which will be the foundation of the development plan.

1503. ID: 255
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities
   Statement: We, the Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities, assert that the profitability of the energy islands is a fundamental requirement, as established in the 2020 Climate Agreement for Energy and Industry. However, we recognize that the economic viability of the Energy Island at Bornholm remains highly uncertain, relying heavily on assumptions about the future development of renewable energy capacity, broader energy systems, and electricity demand both domestically and internationally beyond 2030.

We emphasize that profitability can only be demonstrated under specific scenarios, and even then, it is subject to significant uncertainty. We cannot guarantee that the project will be profitable or free from the need for subsidies. To support decision-making, we have conducted two analyses: a traditional cost-benefit analysis evaluating the societal economic viability of the project as a whole and a supplementary analysis examining the island's cost-effectiveness as infrastructure for consolidating offshore wind energy and facilitating electricity distribution between Denmark and Germany.

In scenarios based on frozen policy assumptions, we find substantial economic deficits for both societal and project finances. However, scenarios that account for partial alignment with renewable energy and electricity demand goals indicate the potential for profitability. These scenarios include contributions from Germany toward transmission costs and anticipated EU financing, which could enable the project to achieve breakeven in societal economic terms.

That said, we acknowledge that the project faces challenges stemming from global volatility in raw material prices and geopolitical uncertainties, such as the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. These factors introduce additional uncertainties regarding the final costs and economic outcomes of the project.

1534. ID: 3816
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Chris Peeters
   Statement: A North Sea grid is cost-effective and helps manage production volatility because wind output varies by location but often follows a predictable pattern. Meteorological phenomena like wind tend to travel across Europe, from the Irish Sea over the North Sea to the Baltic. An energy hub at sea allows wind power to remain offshore until needed by consumers onshore. This island collects wind around it and then brings it to shore or to another hub that delivers it to the country with demand at that time. This approach prevents overloading the land grid, a common issue where Germany pays Danish wind producers to turn off turbines to avoid straining the grid.

1536. ID: 3819
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ulrik Stridsbaek
   Statement: There is currently one hybrid cable in operation in Europe, connecting several wind farms in the Baltic Sea to both Denmark and Germany. This project is operated by Energinet and German grid operator 50Hertz, of which Elia owns 80%. Hybrid projects combine generation and transmission elements and connect two or more markets, unlike traditional offshore wind farms that send power to shore via individual cables to a single country.

The big problem is that all parties must have the incentive to join the development of hybrid projects, and that is not currently the case. Current regulation does not allow for the necessary sharing of costs and revenue that would incentivize all parties to invest. Despite this, Ørsted, which has built roughly a quarter of the world's wind farms at sea, sees hybrid projects as crucial to unlocking offshore wind's future potential. We think that hybrids can be a huge saving of time, money, and hassle.

Renewable electricity offers transformative opportunities for transport, cities, and ports. From a shipping company’s perspective, renewable electricity facilitates shore power, battery charging, and the supply of hydrogen (H₂) and e-fuels. Port infrastructure supports energy supply, hydrogen production via electrolysis, and e-fuel production and storage, such as ammonia and methanol. From the perspective of ports, cities, and communities, renewable electricity enhances grid services and market flexibility, with ports acting as virtual power plants. These integrated systems supply energy for battery charging, hydrogen, and e-fuels, supporting urban and community energy needs."

1559. ID: 1563
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: Energy islands are essentially expensive offshore transformers that collect and condition electricity from offshore wind turbines. These islands do not produce energy but instead consume energy in the process. Electricity from wind turbines, which convert only 10% to 30% of raw wind power into electricity, is sent to the energy island and converted from alternating current to direct current, resulting in about a 15% energy loss. This electricity is then transmitted via undersea cables to land, where it is converted back to alternating current, causing another 15% loss, before being sent to customers. Denmark, for example, generates more electricity by burning American wood chips as biomass than from all its wind turbines and solar panels combined. Globally, over the past decade, more than $5 trillion has been spent on the energy transition, yet wind and solar power contribute less than 5% of total energy consumption—a small achievement while economies face financial strain.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1579. ID: 6558
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: T. M. I. Riayatsyah
   Statement: The industrial revolution drastically transformed the world, leading to massive emissions from human activities. These actions have pushed the exploitation of Earth's natural resources to near irreversible limits. The consequences are evident in the extreme climate changes affecting many countries globally.  

One major contributor to climate change is energy generation, predominantly powered by fossil fuels such as coal and diesel. This process releases significant amounts of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, which accelerates global warming. If fossil fuel consumption continues at its current pace, the planet faces catastrophic outcomes within a few decades.  

To address this issue, scientists and practitioners advocate for environmentally friendly energy alternatives. Renewable energy sources like hydropower, wind, and solar are increasingly promoted to power daily activities sustainably.  

Renewable energy has been extensively adopted in developed nations like the US, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Turkey, and the UK, where it is actively replacing harmful fossil fuels. However, in developing countries like Indonesia, renewable energy remains less popular due to the affordability of electricity from fossil fuels. For instance, Indonesia's energy mix in 2020 heavily favored fossil fuels, highlighting the need for policies and efforts to demonstrate the reliability of renewable energy as a viable alternative.  

Experiences from developed nations show that renewable energy is just as reliable as fossil fuel power plants. Additionally, new data reveals that renewable energy is now cheaper than fossil fuels in terms of levelized cost of energy (CoE), emphasizing its economic and environmental advantages.

1580. ID: 6561
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)

   Statement: Lithuania's approach to energy security has been remarkably consistent in several ways. The country faces an ongoing supply gap in domestic energy production. Lithuanian policymakers and stakeholders, including myself, have typically viewed energy security through a geopolitical lens. For many years, nuclear power was widely seen as the primary solution to Lithuania's energy supply challenges, while renewable energy was not considered a serious near-term option for achieving energy security. However, I observed a dramatic shift around 2015-2016. At this point, renewable energy suddenly emerged as the main strategy for addressing Lithuania's domestic energy production gap. Meanwhile, support for nuclear power waned significantly, culminating in the new government's quiet decision to freeze the Visaginas nuclear project in 2016.

1599. ID: 2186
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Ministry of the Environment
   Statement: The construction work will involve the handling and storage of soil along the cable corridor/trench and at the station areas. The excavated soil along the cable corridor will be reused, meaning there will be no surplus soil that needs to be disposed of. At the station areas, the majority of the excavated soil will be reused. Surplus soil that is not reused will be managed according to a soil management plan approved by the relevant municipality. Any potentially contaminated soil or soil subject to area classification within the project area will also be managed according to a soil management plan approved by the municipality.

The project is not expected to impact groundwater protection, but high groundwater levels or rainwater may occur during the construction period and will need to be temporarily diverted. This water will be managed without affecting the water environment.

Accidents during the construction period, such as unintended seepage of drilling mud from controlled horizontal drilling, could cause direct and indirect impacts on surface water, groundwater, soil, and nature.

1601. ID: 2188
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Ministry of the Environment
   Statement: During the construction phase, the excavation area and construction work will be visible along the cable corridor. Once the construction work is completed, all areas will be restored, and replanting can occur in areas where vegetation had to be cleared. A cable trench will be dug within the work area, approximately 1.5 meters deep and 2.1 meters wide at the top, narrowing to about 1.2 meters at the bottom. The construction work will not take place along the entire length of the cable corridor simultaneously but will occur in smaller sections. From the start of construction on a specific parcel or section to the final restoration of the work area, the process is expected to take 3-5 weeks.

There are no accurate visualizations for either the onshore facility or the offshore wind turbines. We are concerned that Bornholm will end up being turned into an industrial island. 

We can accept the wind turbines at sea because transitioning to more renewable energy is unavoidable. However, we are puzzled as to why Energy Island Bornholm is not being designed like the one in the North Sea, where everything is built far offshore.  

So far, we have felt completely unheard. That is why we have now organized ourselves into an association, hoping that this will give us a stronger voice.

   Statement: The energy islands mark the beginning of a new era for the generation of energy from offshore wind, aimed at creating a green energy supply for Danish and foreign electricity grids. Operating as green power plants at sea, the islands are expected to play a major role in the phasing-out of fossil fuel energy sources in Denmark and Europe. 
After political agreement on the energy islands have been reached, the Danish Energy Agency plays a key role in leading the project that will transform the two energy islands from a vision to reality. The islands are pioneer projects that will necessitate the deployment of existing knowledge into an entirely new context. 
In the Baltic Sea, the electrotechnical equipment will be placed on the island of Bornholm, where electricity from offshore wind farms will be routed to electricity grids on Zealand and neighbouring countries. The offshore wind farms will be established approximately 15 km south-southwest of the coast and will be visible to the naked eye, but not dominate the horizon. The turbines off the coast of Bornholm will have an installed production capacity of up to 3,8 GW including overplanting. 
The location of the new windfarm is quite close to Bornholm and to Bornholm´s Airport at the South-Western corner of the island. Bornholm´s Airport is Denmark´s only state-owned airport administered by Trafikstyrelsen and operated by a local management team. The airport is as mentioned above located in the South Western corner of Bornholm with the coordinates 55°03′48″N 014°45′34″Ø close to Rønne town and to the sea in the western direction of the new windfarms. 
The airport has a 2002 m long and 45 m wide runway and service all kinds of aviation comprising: Scheduled passenger traffic mainly to Copenhagen, Charter traffic, Cargo traffic, General Aviation traffic (GA traffic), Search and Rescue traffic (SAR traffic), Military surveillance traffic. 
The airport is counted among the smaller airports in Denmark and had in 2021 180.000 arriving and departing passengers heavily influenced by the Corona pandemic. 
The location of Bornholm 1 and 2 will not interfere with the outer horizon for the instrument approach and landings with a 15 km distance between the windfarm and the airport. However, if the northern tip of the windfarm is moved closer to the airport to allow for more wind from the sea it may be necessary to move the upper rows of windmills to another location in the windfarm areas to avoid a conflict with the 15 km outer surface. The above-mentioned analysis of aviation related issues and scope of work will comprise civil traffic, military traffic, helicopter traffic and drone traffic.

1642. ID: 6218
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We believe that it is prudent to maintain the option of overplanting for offshore wind on the Energy Islands. While overplanting does not increase the overall amount of electricity delivered to the grid beyond the production permit, it can offset transmission losses between turbines and the connection point. Additionally, overplanting can compensate for the occasional downtime of turbines due to maintenance or other factors, which can reduce the overall output of the wind farm. We want to clarify that overplanting will occur within the existing designated area for offshore wind farms, specifically within a maximum distance of 15 kilometers from the coast. To implement overplanting, wind farm developers will need to place turbines closer together than initially planned. If our environmental assessment indicates that a plan for 3.8 GW can be implemented without significant impacts, we would then allow wind farm developers to choose the economically optimal capacity within a range of 3.2 to 3.8 GW.

1645. ID: 1900
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Energy islands as a cornerstone in Europe’s green transition
   Actor: Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities
   Statement: We firmly believe that the development of offshore wind in the North Sea is a vital step toward electrifying Denmark and Europe. As we move toward a future where renewable energy sources must account for a much larger share of our energy consumption, we see this as a pivotal solution. By transitioning to green electricity, we can significantly reduce our dependence on fossil fuels, including Russian oil, coal, and gas.

The energy islands, which include artificial islands (such as Denmark’s energy island in the North Sea) and technical facilities on existing islands (like the energy island planned for Bornholm), represent a breakthrough in energy infrastructure. These islands will connect surrounding offshore wind farms to the electricity grids of multiple countries, enabling the distribution of green electricity directly to households and businesses across borders.

We are convinced that energy islands will enable the production of green electricity on an unprecedented scale. This innovation will help phase out fossil fuel-based energy production and pave the way for a more sustainable energy future. To ensure a reliable energy supply, even in a renewable-energy-driven system dependent on weather conditions, it is critical to fully harness the potential of the North Sea. Establishing a robust cross-border energy infrastructure will optimize our wind resources, and energy islands will play a central role in achieving this goal.

Moreover, energy islands will empower Europe to electrify large segments of society while making electricity consumption greener for households and businesses alike. These islands also have immense potential to serve as hubs for energy storage and for converting green electricity into sustainable fuels through Power-to-X technologies. This will provide solutions for heavy transportation sectors, such as aviation and shipping, further advancing our green transition.

We are committed to supporting these developments and ensuring that energy islands become a cornerstone of Europe’s sustainable energy future.

Dialogue means an exchange of viewpoints, especially between conflicting parties, to reach mutual agreement—unlike a unilateral imposition.
We have submitted a citizens’ proposal to Parliament and urge all politicians to take it seriously and do the necessary work to change the law.
We are more than willing to contribute to the work if someone is willing to listen!

1655. ID: 1864
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Local opposition and citizen concerns about Bornholm project
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: I think I love the southern Bornholm landscape. That's why it bothers me that I'll probably be neighbors with the planned transformer station for Energy Island Bornholm.
I live close to the 260-square-meter area southwest of Aakirkeby, which has been designated to house the planned transformer station. I really don't like the idea of changing this peaceful farmland forever.
I’m upset about it. It’s going to change the area completely. It’s going to be a massive, massive construction. I know a bit about construction from my work as a farmer, and 70 to 90 hectares in size and 25 meters in height is huge. Plus, they’ll have to bury a lot of cables. I often drive past the area on my way to Rønne, and it’s a bit frightening to imagine the quiet, peaceful farmland being dug up by big excavators and something so large being built.
I moved back to Bornholm because I wanted to live where I grew up and see things develop slowly and peacefully. I have no problem with small agricultural buildings being built, or a house being removed or built. But these are not the huge changes you move to Bornholm for—especially not to southern Bornholm.
I’ll probably have to look at that transformer station for the rest of my life. There will be a before and an after. The untouched nature, the way things have just continued as they have for generations—it’s just over.
I own land, and maybe the value of the land in the area will rise because there’ll be less of it. So, we might end up making a lot of money from it. But I would have preferred it if that hadn’t been the case.
We could get electrification for the Bornholm community that we wouldn’t otherwise have had. It’s also good that there’ll be less CO2 emissions and hopefully a lot of jobs.

1665. ID: 1710
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Rasmus Errboe
   Statement: Together with ATP,  we have developed a proposal for the energy island that a political majority wants to establish in the North Sea. 

The proposal can be described as a model that can be built upon as needs or technology change. 

Specifically, ATP and Ørsted propose building a smaller version of an artificial island. It can then gradually be expanded with new modules, such as those that make it possible to send offshore wind energy to land. 

According to us, it can be compared to building with LEGO bricks, where one can build and build on top of a foundation. 

The fundamental idea of our proposal is that it should be modular 

You build a relatively small enclosed island, where you then work with modules around the island that can be installed in connection with the island over time, as technological development changes.

1707. ID: 6052

   Actor: Per Nikolaj Bukh
   Statement: The Energy Island project at Bornholm is facing significant challenges due to unclear legal regulations, allowing competing offshore wind farms to establish themselves adjacent to the planned Energy Island. This oversight by the Danish Energy Agency is described as "catastrophic" by Per Nikolaj Bukh, a professor of economic management at Aalborg University. Specifically, two applications to set up wind farms in the Bornholm Bassin South and East, totaling three gigawatts, are in direct competition with the planned capacity of Energy Island, leading to a larger supply of electricity and consequently lower electricity prices. 1710. ID: 6051
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Peter Ejler
   Statement: Ørsted, as a potential developer of offshore wind farms, is represented by Peter Ejler, senior lead procurement manager. He emphasizes that Ørsted must comply with the EU's Energy Security Directive, which prevents offering preferential treatment based on the location of companies, such as prioritizing Bornholm-based businesses.

Ørsted maintains a supplier database with 22,000 registered companies, and in order to be considered, companies must meet a series of criteria. These requirements help ensure that contractors and their subcontractors are capable of handling safety, investing in training, obtaining ISO certifications, and being commercially competitive—not only on price but also in terms of reliability and flexibility.

In return, Ørsted is committed to playing an active role in local communities by contributing to fundraising efforts, offering sponsorships, and organizing networking events to connect contractors with local suppliers.

As a rule of thumb, Ørsted states that 1 gigawatt of offshore wind generates 10,000 jobs, a benefit that extends far beyond Bornholm. However, if companies can meet the necessary criteria, there will be local job opportunities within the wind farms. Peter Ejler highlights that there are significant opportunities for local businesses to help service the wind farms, mentioning that Rønne Harbor is particularly important as a key shipping and supply hub for the wind turbines.

Energy islands, which will be located in the Baltic Sea at Bornholm and in the North Sea with an artificial island, are designed to significantly increase the production of renewable energy. 1737. ID: 1180
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Peter K. Kruse-Andersen
   Statement: I highlight a coordination problem between the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy. I exemplify this coordination failure by analyzing carbon leakage effects associated with Denmark's planned North Sea energy island. The Danish energy island project will not start production before 2033, implying a long interval between project announcement and production. Using a dynamic model of the EU ETS, I show that the large time gap between announcement and production likely results in a ‘Green Paradox’, where the energy island increases aggregate EU ETS emissions. The mechanism leading to the emission increase is complicated and works through the Market Stability Reserve (MSR). The estimated 2050 leakage rate is 145 percent in our main scenario and not below 100 percent in any alternative scenario. We discuss how to improve the climate benefits of the energy island or similar large-scale renewable energy projects. This includes possible revisions to the EU ETS and the role of Power-to-X technologies.

There is a coordination failure between the EU ETS and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy, as projects intended to fulfil the offshore strategy are likely to result in substantial carbon leakage due to the EU ETS.
In ETS-covered sectors, there are averse leakage effects associated with emission abatement projects with significant time lags between project announcements and emission abatement like the Danish North Sea energy island.
For the North Sea energy island and similar projects, leakage effects can be diminished through policies that mitigate the impact on EU ETS allowance demand.
The coordination failure can be eliminated by removing MSR cancellations or the entire MSR mechanism while adjusting the emission cap to hold expected emissions constant.
However, removing MSR cancellations amplifies leakage effects for abatement projects with short time lags between announcements and emission abatement, which currently have weak leakage effects due to MSR cancellations.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1761. ID: 5384
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: The concept of islands – historically seen as places of desire – is growing in relevance. Alongside natural islands, artificial ones are now being created. Denmark is currently planning the construction of an energy island in the North Sea, recognizing that the North Sea is the only genuinely large and reliable green power source in Europe. Is this a revolutionary concept? Not entirely. Similar visions for expanding Scharhörn into a significant energy hub in Hamburg arose during the 1960s oil crisis, known as the "Labskausdeal." Back then, the CEO of Salzgitter noted that no one in the steel industry could ignore Scharhörn.

For other Nordic nations, the idea proved too visionary and expensive, which led many energy-intensive companies from North Rhine-Westphalia to relocate to Belgium and the Netherlands. For Hamburg, this shift led to a focus on the Elbe metropolis and HafenCity with numerous river deepening projects, alongside a multi-billion-euro dredging operation funded by German taxpayers, yet lacking a genuine future outlook.

Now, Cuxhaven is positioning itself to capitalize on this opportunity for the northern countries with an island project that addresses the crucial challenges of today. We can eagerly anticipate the creation of the new, multifunctional "Watt'n Stoff Bundesinsel" (Federal Island).

The development of offshore meshed grids faces several critical challenges. First, more resilient supply chains are needed. Second, better long-term visibility of project developments are required.

European governments have set ambitious offshore wind targets, but WindEurope insists that grid development deserves equal attention. 1829. ID: 7009
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jacob Østergaard
   Statement: Producing hydrogen at a scale of 1 GW requires approximately 1.8 million cubic meters of water annually. This water must be ultrapure, necessitating extensive treatment before seawater can be used. Additionally, high-quality cooling water is required due to the significant generation of waste heat during hydrogen production. A major technical challenge involves designing pipelines suitable for both hydrogen transport and corrosive seawater environments.

Current state-of-the-art seawater desalination technologies, such as reverse osmosis, are complex, require high maintenance, and consume significant amounts of energy. However, thermal integration of electrolyzers with seawater desalination processes could create a more dynamic and efficient system capable of handling the fluctuating water demands for future offshore hydrogen production.

An alternative approach would be developing electrolysis technologies capable of tolerating salt or seawater directly. However, a key challenge is that hydrogen interacts with many metals, expanding their lattice structure and compromising mechanical integrity under high pressure.

There is a critical need for further research in two areas: the development of reliable, efficient, and compact seawater desalination systems, and the creation of advanced materials that are both corrosion-resistant and capable of maintaining structural integrity under high hydrogen pressures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1832. ID: 3808
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Emmanuel Grasland
   Statement: The main issue with wind farms is that the cost of their electrical infrastructure increases dramatically as the distance from the shore grows. Alternating current isn’t suitable for long-distance transmission, so we need to use direct current, which requires much more expensive substations and cables. That’s where energy islands come in—they completely change the game. By centralizing and sharing electrical infrastructure, like transformers and cables, between turbines and the mainland, energy islands reduce the overall investment needed. Plus, they allow electricity to be distributed to multiple countries instead of being tied to a single national grid. This makes it easier to sell the electricity at the best price when the turbines are running at full capacity, without risking disruptions to any one grid.

1850. ID: 5330

   Statement: The new geopolitical and energy market landscape has accelerated the green transition. The European Commission's RePowerEU plan aims to make Europe independent from Russian fossil fuels by 2030, prioritizing renewable energy, energy efficiency, and diversification. Combined with the European Green Deal and NextGenerationEU (NGEU) funding, these initiatives form a powerful foundation for sustainable energy development. However, islands face a unique energy challenge.

Islands struggle with higher electricity generation costs, often ten times greater than on the mainland, due to their size, isolation, and reliance on fossil fuel imports. They are also more prone to power outages. Despite these challenges, islands have long pursued sustainable solutions, driven by innovation, collaboration, and community effort, frequently utilizing cutting-edge technology. In many ways, islands serve as testing grounds for sustainable practices that could be scaled to larger, mainland communities. As the world grapples with the energy crisis, islands offer a potential blueprint for overcoming energy challenges.

1872. ID: 3551
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Claus Leth Bak
   Statement: The energy island is designed to connect to the grid via a multiterminal high-voltage direct current (MTHVDC) system—a concept still untested on the scale required for onshore grids. Existing MTHVDC systems have limitations unsuitable for energy islands, highlighting the need for research, development, and standardization efforts from suppliers and operators.

Rushing the project risks dependency on a single supplier, complicating future tenders and integration of new technologies. A failure in the MTHVDC system would harm project economics and reduce green energy availability.

Historically, grid development has been incremental, enabling adaptation. Implementing a large-scale system all at once risks durability issues, as untested replacements and interactions between old and new equipment may create challenges.

1879. ID: 4831
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Job creation and innovation
   Actor: Claus M. Andersen
   Statement: This might be the most groundbreaking project we’ve landed in the 15 years we’ve hosted research and demonstration projects.

The Combined Heat and Power Plant on Skansevej in Rønne will soon house the Second Life for Powerplants project.

A number of European pioneers in energy technology have teamed up to solve one of the biggest challenges in sustainable transition: capturing and storing energy from solar and wind power, ensuring electricity and heat are available even on cloudy, windless days. The project budget is DKK 100 million, with EU support amounting to DKK 60 million.

The idea behind Second Life for Powerplants is to repurpose existing power plant technology while building on employees' skills. This means reusing the steam turbine, generator, control systems, and connections to the electricity grid and district heating network. The power plant will be equipped with three new storage technologies: a salt storage system, used electric vehicle batteries, and a high-tech flywheel battery. At the core of the concept is an advanced control software designed to ensure the availability of electricity and heat – even on overcast days with no wind.

"We will gain invaluable knowledge about how to handle and store solar and wind energy in the future – and how to effectively ensure balance in the electricity system. We will obtain solid insights into what it takes to fully utilize solar and wind power without significantly increasing costs for Bornholm’s residents. We will also get clear indications of the investments required to finally say goodbye to oil and phase out wood chips," I explained.

I also pointed out that the experiences gained from the project on Bornholm can be easily replicated elsewhere, making it much easier, cheaper, and faster to convert, for instance, a Polish coal power plant into a flexible energy storage facility for solar and wind power.

"The fact that we could land such a project on Bornholm might suggest that we should consider raising our expectations about the additional activity the Bornholm Energy Island will generate for the island," I concluded.

Energy island technology is, therefore, essential, and if I do not use Denmark’s head start with Energy Island Bornholm to turn it into a Danish strength, other countries will simply take the lead.

Security is on everyone’s mind. How do I ensure that the new large facilities and the connections I will depend on in the future are protected from terrorism and hybrid warfare? During the meeting, these topics were discussed, and I explained that at my upcoming Baltic Energy Island Summit, I would focus on the issue.

A big thank you for the visit!

1890. ID: 3514

That fuel must be in demand, and the vehicles and machinery powered by it must be ready—either specifically designed for the purpose or modified so their engines can run on sustainable fuels.

If this development does not happen quickly enough, there will be too much electricity for the grid. This would require further reinforcement of the grid, which is already expensive. According to a report by the consultancy Rambøll from March 7 this year (2023), the grid expansion will cost 110 billion kroner, which is 30 billion more than estimated in 2020. Such a significant expansion also takes time, and it is doubtful whether it can be completed in time.

Meanwhile, the large amounts of surplus electricity from the energy island during periods of high wind would either go to waste or be sold at extremely low prices. For instance, one cannot simply rely on exporting to Germany, which is also undergoing a significant expansion of offshore wind farms.

1906. ID: 4803
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The framework for Denmark’s largest offshore wind tender in history has been established. I could potentially secure green electricity for more than 14 million Danish and European households, and for the first time, I would be part of the ownership. The agreement also contributes to energy security, and better marine environments are ensured through the upcoming Marine Nature Fund.

The government and parties such as SF, Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party, the Red-Green Alliance, the Social Liberal Party, the Danish People’s Party, and the Alternative have reached an agreement that sets the framework for Denmark’s largest offshore wind expansion of 9 GW, which could potentially grow to 14 GW or more, provided I make use of the flexibility in the agreement to build the maximum possible capacity on the allocated areas. These wind farms could contribute substantial amounts of green energy to Denmark and Europe, as well as to PtX products like green hydrogen.

Last year, a broad majority in the Danish Parliament entered into a climate agreement for a greener and more secure Denmark, and in 2020, an agreement was made on Energy Island Bornholm for 2 GW, later expanded to 3 GW. Together with additional GW from the 2018 Energy Agreement and the 2022 Finance Act, the goal of tendering a total of 9 GW was established. While previous agreements set high ambitions, this agreement defines the specific framework to turn goals into actions.

Now it is up to the market to realize the projects that must ensure strengthened green and secure energy supply and help make Denmark and Europe free from fossil energy from Russia and other states.

And because the offshore wind market has become much more favorable in recent years, the agreement ensures that society also gets a share of the common resource, which is Denmark’s maritime area. This happens through bidders’ concession payments combined with the state’s 20 percent co-ownership of the 6 GW tenders.

“This agreement makes Denmark greener. When the turbines spin, I can cover all of my electricity consumption with green power – even to such an extent that I can also contribute to Europe’s green transition and energy security. I can now finally give the market the green light for the expansion of potentially 14 GW of offshore wind or more – and for the first time, I and the state will become co-owners of most of them, thereby gaining a share of the actual revenues from offshore wind. I am introducing new sustainability requirements and establishing a Marine Nature Fund, so nature is also considered. The next chapter must now be written in collaboration with market actors, as they are the ones who must take the lead,” says Climate, Energy, and Utilities Minister Lars Aagaard.

“I have entered into a broad agreement that sets the framework for a historically large expansion of green electricity. Denmark’s maritime areas will become a driving force in the green transition – not just in Denmark, but across Europe. The agreement will also strengthen energy security and support Danish strengths and jobs. At the same time, it will contribute to making Europe more independent of, for example, Russian gas. Finally, the agreement ensures that society as a whole benefits from the returns on Denmark’s wind resources,” says Acting Minister for Economic Affairs Stephanie Lose.

“This is, in every way, a historic day. With this agreement, I am utilizing and developing my strengths in offshore wind on a historic scale. This must happen in cooperation between the state and the business sector. And it will be very concrete: The agreement parties agree that the state should be a co-owner of the individual offshore wind farms. To ensure that the Danish society gets a fair share of future revenues when our shared maritime resource is used for offshore wind. Co-ownership is a stamp of confidence for developers that the government wants to invest in the green transition – together with them and for the benefit of society as a whole,” says Minister for Business Morten Bødskov.

1968. ID: 1841
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Søren Møller Christensen
   Statement: I have been asked several times how it makes sense to produce power-to-x on Bornholm. Wouldn't it make much more sense to transport electricity to Copenhagen or Berlin and convert it into, for example, jet fuels in those locations, where there are also large cities with extensive district heating networks that can absorb the significant amounts of heat? It’s a logical question.

The issue, however, is that transporting electricity through cables is expensive, while transporting hydrogen through pipelines is cheaper. In other words, from an economic perspective, it makes the most sense to produce hydrogen as close to the energy source as possible. This is reflected in the fact that wind turbine manufacturers are working on developing turbines that, in the future, will produce hydrogen directly inside the turbine or on platforms near the turbines. In these turbines, most of the heat will be lost, but they are expected to be cost-effective because the electricity is converted to hydrogen very close to the energy source.

However, this type of turbine will not be used for Energy Island Bornholm, as the primary focus is on electricity production, and the new turbine type is not expected to be ready until the 2030s.

Regarding the question of why it is relevant to produce hydrogen on Bornholm, it is also worth noting that Bornholm is not the only community grappling with what power-to-x means for them. Green fuels, particularly hydrogen, are part of the vision in most places where there are plans for major expansions of wind and solar energy—and often, these are in smaller communities far from major cities. For example, this is also the case for the two other energy islands in the Baltic Sea, Gotland and Åland. Åland, in particular, is far along in its plans to produce hydrogen based on the 4–6 GW of offshore wind that can be developed in the waters around the archipelago.

I am often asked whether power-to-x makes economic sense. The think tank Kraka has, for example, published a report arguing that building a power-to-x industry in Denmark will require substantial financial support because green fuels are currently more expensive than fossil fuels. Both the question and the argument are logical, but they do not change the fact that power-to-x is an essential part of the solution to the climate crisis. Moreover, there is political recognition of the need to find ways to enable the commercial production of green fuels.

This can happen through support from the Danish state or the EU, which is already occurring today. In the future, it is also expected to happen through additional taxes based on the amount of CO₂ emitted by a particular type of production, making CO₂-neutral fuels more competitive compared to, for instance, coal and oil.

Whether power-to-x is supported directly through subsidies or indirectly through CO₂ taxes, the energy sector expects power-to-x to play a crucial role in the green transition. Furthermore, there is significant political focus in Denmark on making power-to-x a new area of national industrial strength.

1970. ID: 1839
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Michael Stoltze
   Statement: The transition from climate-damaging to climate-neutral energy sources is fraught with challenges, including the massive scale of the required infrastructure. Bornholm’s geographical position in a critical sea area for renewable energy delivery to Northern Europe places the island in the middle of a significant dilemma.

While we recognize the uncertain economic feasibility of these large-scale projects, we are particularly concerned about their potential impact on Bornholm’s nature and landscape. These are foundational values for Bornholm and the main reasons for its popularity, which must not be jeopardized.

As Danmarks Naturfredningsforening Bornholm, our primary goal is to protect and improve nature, the environment, and the landscape. We fully support the green transition to a society that avoids pollution, stabilizes the climate, preserves nature, and protects landscapes. A blanket rejection of all development, including wind turbines and solar farms, is not a viable option. Effective environmental solutions are essential to address pollution and climate change while maintaining the integrity of nature and the landscape.

For the massive land-based energy infrastructure planned on Bornholm, we demand the highest standards and will not compromise. This will be the largest construction project in Bornholm’s history, occupying a small percentage of the island’s area but having a visible impact due to the height of the structures. Therefore, it must be situated in a way that minimizes harm to nature and the landscape. The design should incorporate architecture, vegetation, and earthworks to integrate harmoniously into the surroundings.

The proposed location north of Søndre Landevej, although not without issues, is the best option available. The site is primarily agricultural land with low natural value, flat terrain, and a location sufficiently distant from the scenic south coast. While the project will affect farmland and buildings, the surrounding natural environment can be enhanced through thoughtful design. The plan includes low vegetation, bushes, and trees between the buildings, as well as tree lines and the restoration of a small stream, which will increase the area’s biodiversity compared to its current state.

However, we emphasize the need for varied-height earthen berms around the site. These berms will reduce the visual dominance of the large buildings and provide habitats for diverse flora and fauna by creating microclimates. Additionally, the berms can be used for walking trails, offering both scenic views and access to nature.

Nature and the landscape must not be sacrificed. This project is a significant opportunity to develop a solution that benefits Bornholm while serving as a national and international model for integrating renewable energy development with respect for nature and the landscape. This is the challenge we face, and we are committed to making it a success.

1988. ID: 361
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: WindEurope
   Statement: The North Sea has the potential to host more than 200 offshore wind farms, each with a capacity of 1 GW, due to its strong winds and shallow waters. However, achieving this requires building wind farms far from the coast, which significantly increases the cost of electrical infrastructure. Alternating current does not transmit efficiently over long distances, necessitating the use of more expensive direct current substations and cabling.

Building an energy island transforms this scenario. An energy island allows for the pooling of electrical infrastructure—such as transformers and cables—connecting the wind farms to the mainland, thereby reducing the required investment. Additionally, an energy island enables the delivery of electricity to multiple countries instead of a single national grid. This makes it easier to sell electricity at the best price when wind farms are operating at full capacity, without risking instability in any single grid.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1995. ID: 4567
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The seabed is an important habitat for animals and plants. The implementation of the Plan for Program Energy Bornholm could potentially impact the geological and geomorphological characteristics of the seabed due to changes in its composition and structure. This impact could result from activities such as excavation and the establishment of fixed structures like wind turbine foundations during the development of offshore wind farms.

The seabed's geological composition in the two planned areas for offshore wind primarily consists of clay deposits interspersed with layers of sand and gravel. The topography of the seabed in the planned area is characterized by generally shallow water depths ranging from 0 to 55 meters.

Our marine strategy sets goals for the integrity of the seabed, ensuring that the extent of habitat loss caused by human activity and the degree of negative effects remain within a certain percentage of the natural habitat's distribution in the assessment area.

Regarding the total area of seabed types affected, the implementation of the plan will not result in the involvement of rare or vulnerable seabed types. Therefore, the total permanently affected seabed area will be minimal compared to the total seabed area. Consequently, the degree of impact is assessed as moderate, and the effect on the seabed and topography is not considered significant.

1997. ID: 4566
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The realization of the Energy Island Bornholm Plan may lead to potential impacts on fish and fish populations due to habitat changes and displacement from living areas caused by increased sediment in the water column. The construction of foundations on the seabed and the laying of submarine cables could result in permanent and temporary alterations to the seabed, potentially affecting feeding grounds, spawning areas, and nursery habitats for fish. During construction activities such as foundation excavation and cable laying, increased concentrations of suspended sediment in the water column may occur, which could displace fish that rely on vision for hunting and feeding. Additionally, electromagnetic fields (EMF) from energized submarine cables may have localized potential impacts on fish that are particularly sensitive to EMF.

However, the potential impacts of elevated sediment concentrations on fish, fish eggs, and larvae during construction are expected to be local, short-term, and of low intensity, comparable to those observed in similar offshore wind projects. Overall, the impact level is assessed as insignificant, and the effect on fish populations is not considered significant.

The impact on fish due to habitat changes from the installation of turbines and cables is assessed as negligible and not significant, as the structures represent a limited area of the overall soft-bottom substrate. Excluding commercial fishing in the planned areas and along the cables is expected to have a small positive impact on local fish populations in the area. Consequently, the overall impact on fish is assessed as negligible and not significant. Fish potentially affected by EMF from buried submarine cables are only expected to experience minimal impacts, as the cables will be buried 1 meter below the seabed, and the EMF exposure at the surface is very low. This potential impact is assessed as being very localized, within a few meters of the cables, and of low intensity and permanent duration. Overall, the impact is considered negligible and not significant for fish populations.

   Cluster: (None)

   Statement: The realization of the Plan for the Energy Island Bornholm program will permanently allocate areas for offshore wind turbines and temporarily allocate areas for cable installation. Additionally, the intensity of the potential impact will be influenced by the vulnerability of local species, particularly concerning sediment spills and hydrographic conditions.

2000. ID: 4562
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Danish Energy Agency acknowledges that the construction activities related to the "Energy Island" project in the Baltic Sea, such as noise from the installation of wind turbine foundations and vessel traffic, could potentially impact two seal species: harbor seals and gray seals. 

Harbor seals are unlikely to be significantly affected as there are no breeding grounds near the planned offshore wind farm area, and the density of harbor seals in the vicinity is very low. Underwater noise is therefore expected to primarily affect gray seals. 

Measures to manage noise will ensure that gray seals are not at risk of permanent or even temporary hearing loss, as gray seals are not expected to be within 5 km of the construction area. Behavioral changes among gray seals may occur during the winter within a range of up to 6.5 km from the construction area. The noise impact from monopile installation, even with mitigation measures, is assessed as a local effect of moderate intensity and long duration. However, the overall impact is evaluated as moderate and not significant.

2020. ID: 4560
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Natura 2000 areas are designated based on European nature protection directives and are part of the EU's international network of habitat and bird protection areas. Each Natura 2000 area has a specific designation basis, listing habitat types and species meant for protection. 

The realization of the "Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan" may affect certain habitat types and species in several Natura 2000 areas. A materiality assessment was conducted for all relevant Natura 2000 areas, including those with migratory birds as part of their designation basis. This assessment incorporated standard noise-reduction measures in modeling underwater noise from pile driving. 

The conclusion of the materiality assessment is that significant displacement effects on harbor porpoises due to underwater noise cannot be ruled out. However, no other habitat types or species designated for protection would be significantly affected. 

A subsequent impact assessment for harbor porpoises, where significant effects could not initially be ruled out, concluded that the species would not be harmed if pile driving occurs no closer than 5–7 kilometers from the affected Natura 2000 areas during winter (November through April). In the summer, pile driving must not involve more than one foundation at a time near the habitat areas, as simultaneous pile driving could increase the area and duration of porpoise displacement.

The final conclusion of the impact assessment is that the realization of the "Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan," whether on its own or in combination with other projects, poses no risk of harm to harbor porpoises or the integrity of the Natura 2000 areas. This conclusion assumes the implementation of all relevant mitigation measures in future projects. Therefore, the integrity of Natura 2000 areas will not be compromised by the realization of the program plan.

2026. ID: 4347
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The Energiø Bornholm project, which aims to create a three-gigawatt energy island, requires a state subsidy of 31.5 billion kroner over 20 years to cover its projected economic deficit of 12 billion kroner. This translates to nearly 1.6 billion kroner annually in support and represents 10.5 billion kroner per gigawatt. Initially, the project was planned to be self-financing, but updated assessments reveal that state funding is necessary.

The increased cost stems from adjustments to align the energy island’s design with future climate goals and a political decision to expand its capacity from two to three gigawatts. The 31.5 billion kroner subsidy corresponds to half the cost of constructing and operating the approximately 200 offshore wind turbines around Bornholm and the cable connecting them to Zealand’s electricity grid.

I, Lars Aagaard, Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities, recognize the need for further clarification regarding the project’s finances and funding requirements. These financial details are currently under discussion with the parliamentary agreement parties in the negotiation room. 

While some critics, such as Gunnar Olesen from Vedvarende Energi, argue that taxpayers should not bear the cost, pointing out that solar and onshore wind projects require no state subsidies, the Energiø Bornholm project is part of broader political negotiations to double offshore wind capacity in other parts of Denmark, resulting in a quadrupling of the current capacity nationwide. The Energiø Bornholm project remains integral to Denmark’s climate and energy ambitions.

2027. ID: 4318
   Year: 2023

   Statement: We at the Danish Environmental Protection Agency explain that, following this supplementary consultation, the landfall point at Vallø Strand has been excluded, and the cable route from Snoldelev-Hastrup to Vallø Strand has been removed. These changes reduce the cable system's length from approximately 30 km to around 8 km. The cables will be installed as underground cables leading to the new high-voltage stations. For most sections, the cables will be buried, but in particularly sensitive areas, such as at watercourse crossings or vulnerable natural sites, the cables will be laid using directional drilling to avoid excavation and minimize environmental impact.

2032. ID: 4578
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We acknowledges that some components in high-voltage systems may contain potent greenhouse gases, such as SF6 (sulfur hexafluoride), commonly used in high-voltage components over 100 kV and as an insulating medium in Gas Insulated Switchgear (GIS). SF6 is a powerful greenhouse gas, 25,200 times more potent than CO₂ and with an atmospheric lifespan of 3,200 years. Emissions occur during filling, leaks, and similar processes.

The implementation of the Energy Island Bornholm program will enable the construction of high-voltage systems on Bornholm and Zealand, which may lead to unintended emissions of SF6 during operation. However, the anticipated emissions are assessed as having no significant climate impact due to their limited contribution relative to municipal and national carbon inventories. Over time, SF6 will be gradually replaced with alternatives that have a lower climate footprint. If future high-voltage systems are built using SF6 and the estimated emissions occur, the negative effects can be mitigated by utilizing agricultural land. Overall, the impact on the climate is expected to be minimal, and the plan's realization may result in a small net positive effect.

2039. ID: 4574
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The realization of the Energy Island Bornholm plan has the potential to affect soil conditions due to the possibility of municipalities altering land use within the planned areas. These potential effects on soil include land appropriation, soil compaction, contamination, and changes to groundwater levels. Experience from similar projects shows that soil impact is most significant during the establishment of high-voltage installations, while the impacts of laying land cables are temporary and less severe.

On both Bornholm and Zealand, there are significant areas with freshwater formations within the planning zones for high-voltage installations. These areas will be further investigated to identify potential deep peat and organic soil zones as part of specific construction considerations. It is assessed that the construction enabled by the plan can proceed without significant impacts.

There are no extensive areas with identified soil contamination within the planned zones for land cables and high-voltage installations. The construction enabled by the plan is considered feasible without a risk of increased contamination spread, including to groundwater, provided any contaminated soil is managed according to current legislation. The risk of increased soil contamination is deemed low, as contaminated sites can be avoided, and any affected soil will be handled according to established guidelines. Overall, it is assessed that there will be no significant impact on soil from the realization of the plan.

On Zealand, several parts of the planned zones for land cables and the landing of submarine cables overlap with lowland areas identified in municipal plans. Guided drilling is used to install cables under lowland areas, which minimizes significant impacts. However, establishing high-voltage installations and other fixed facilities, such as joint bays, on lowland areas may require additional drainage, potentially leading to ochre leakage. Despite this, it is possible to place joint bays outside designated lowland areas to avoid such impacts. High-voltage installations can also be established outside lowland areas on both Zealand and Bornholm. Consequently, the impact on lowland areas is assessed as negligible, and the overall effect is not considered significant.

   Statement: The North Sea energy island project has encountered significant financial challenges. The project, which was supposed to serve as a hub for collecting and distributing electricity from offshore wind turbines located 80–100 kilometers off the west coast of Jutland, is currently estimated to cost the state over 50 billion kroner. This far exceeds the acceptable level of financial viability required by the political agreements that underpin the project.

Given these economic obstacles, the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities will spend the next six months exploring alternative designs to make the project less complex and more affordable. The current model, developed since 2020, has proven to be too costly and risky. To address these issues, I, Lars Aagaard, Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities, am considering lessons from other North Sea countries. These countries have opted for simpler steel structure platforms to reduce costs. Another potential cost-saving measure involves accelerating the construction of some offshore wind turbines, which would generate power for the energy island sooner.

Despite the delays, the government remains committed to the ambition of realizing the North Sea energy island. However, adjustments must be made to ensure the project is economically viable. It is essential to move quickly, as the energy island needs to be operational shortly after 2030 to meet energy goals. We will engage in discussions with businesses, investors, and the Danish Parliament to find viable solutions and proceed responsibly without unnecessary haste.

The challenges are significant, but they reflect the scale and innovation required for a project of this nature, which has never been attempted before.
