2063. ID: 1483
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Siemens Energy
   Statement: In this article, we wish to bring awareness and create some thoughtful conversations surrounding emerging technological philosophies. Specifically, Sector coupling and Power-to-X.

Sector coupling and Power-to-X are two related concepts that have emerged, globally, as key strategies in the transition towards a more sustainable and climate-neutral energy system.

At the forefront of this technological and philosophical advancement is Siemens Energy 

Sector coupling refers to the integration of different energy sectors, such as electricity, heating, cooling, and transportation, in a way that maximizes the efficient use of renewable energy sources. The goal is to create a more flexible, efficient, and resilient energy system that can better accommodate the fluctuations in renewable energy supply.

Power-to-X, on the other hand, refers to the conversion of renewable electricity into other forms of energy, such as hydrogen, synthetic fuels, or chemicals. These energy carriers can be used to decarbonize other sectors, such as transportation, heating, or industry, that are difficult to electrify directly.

Together, sector coupling and Power-to-X can help to create a circular economy of energy, where renewable energy sources are used in a flexible and efficient way to meet the demands of different sectors, while also reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Some examples of sector coupling and Power-to-X applications include:

Power-to-Heat: using excess renewable electricity to produce heat for buildings or industrial processes, through technologies such as heat pumps or electric boilers.
Power-to-Cold: using excess renewable electricity to produce cooling for buildings or industrial processes, through technologies such as absorption chillers.
Power-to-Hydrogen: using renewable electricity to produce hydrogen through electrolysis, which can be used as a fuel for transportation or as a feedstock for industrial processes.
Power-to-Synfuels: using renewable electricity to produce synthetic fuels, such as methanol or synthetic natural gas, that can be used as substitutes for fossil fuels in transportation or industry.

By combining renewable energy sources with innovative technologies for energy conversion and storage, sector coupling and Power-to-X can help to create a more sustainable, reliable, and climate-neutral energy system.

2085. ID: 40

   Statement: Ørsted, ATP, and their partners have presented a concept for the North Sea Energy Island, envisioned as an ever-evolving project even after its initial construction. This dynamic piece of Denmark’s history is designed to be the cornerstone of the green transition.

The North Sea Energy Island will start as a small reclaimed island, expandable with flexible modules that can be added or replaced as needed. These modules are constructed on land and seamlessly connected to the island, enabling scalability to handle more than Denmark's current ambition of 10 gigawatts of offshore wind. This ensures the delivery of an energy island capable of significant offshore wind scaling and prepared for future requirements. The vision is to build more than just an island—a future-proof hub for innovation and adaptation as the green transition progresses.

2095. ID: 4412
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Anne Filbert
   Statement: The establishment of Energy Island Bornholm will result in Denmark creating a third bidding zone, referred to as DK3. This is due to a structural bottleneck in the power transmission network connecting Energy Island Bornholm to Zealand and Germany, as identified by Energinet.  

Energinet’s analysis indicates that the bottleneck necessitates a revision of Denmark's bidding zones. As a result, the Danish Energy Agency has initiated the creation of the new bidding zone, which will include both Energy Island Bornholm and Bornholm itself.  

According to Veronika Fischer, senior economist at Energinet, this decision is a technical one and will have minimal impact on Bornholm's consumers and producers, who can expect only a slight reduction in electricity prices.  

The decision has been informed by consultations with neighboring countries and stakeholder hearings. Additionally, the Danish Energy Agency has notified the European Commission and the Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (Acer) about the establishment of the new bidding zone.

2099. ID: 4558
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The establishment of large offshore wind farms as part of the Energy Island Bornholm project could potentially influence atmospheric conditions, including wind speed, precipitation, and temperature. Studies involving model calculations indicate that wind turbines extract energy from the wind, resulting in lower wind speeds after passing through the turbines.  

Even in extreme weather scenarios, the maximum average temperature change caused by wind turbines is estimated to be 0.5 degrees Celsius at ground level, with minimal changes in absolute humidity up to 60 kilometers from the offshore wind farms. The magnitude and intensity of these impacts are assessed to be small.  

The potential effects on local and regional weather patterns are projected to persist for several decades, classifying the duration as medium-term. Due to the low oxygen content in the marine area near Bornholm, which could be sensitive to localized climate changes, the sensitivity of the affected areas is rated as medium.  

Overall, the implementation of the Energy Island Bornholm project is expected to result in an insignificant level of negative impact on local and regional weather conditions. Therefore, the influence is deemed negligible.

My work examines how different design features, including the island's shape and orientation, could minimize environmental impacts. 2110. ID: 4554
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We acknowledges that the realization of the Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan poses a risk of encountering and impacting chemical and/or conventional weapons on the seabed. The planned areas intersect a known minefield southwest of Bornholm that was mined by the British Air Force during World War II. Additionally, the western part of the planning area overlaps with a former British minefield, German convoy routes from December 1944, and a potential impact area near Stevns Fortet.

The Bornholm II offshore wind turbine area intersects historical transport routes from German ports to dumping zones and borders areas where chemical weapons have previously been recorded. The planning area for subsea cables is adjacent to an emergency dumping zone southwest of Bornholm.

The rate of findings cannot be precisely determined until a specific project design is available and a geophysical screening survey of identified magnetic anomalies is conducted. Based on current assessments, there is a risk of discovering conventional ammunition on the seabed during the realization of the plan.

However, it is considered feasible to avoid these potential impacts through detailed project design for subsea cables and offshore wind turbines within the planning areas. As such, the realization of the Energy Island Bornholm Plan is expected to have an insignificant impact on unexploded ordnance (UXO) and chemical warfare agents (CWA), regardless of whether the 3.2 GW or 3.8 GW alternative is chosen.

It is critical that all necessary safety precautions are implemented when carrying out activities that may disturb the seabed. This includes ensuring that first aid equipment for chemical weapons exposure is always readily available.

2111. ID: 4553
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We acknowledges that Danish marine areas are used for fishing, and the Plan for the Energy Island at Bornholm may restrict fishing activities in these areas. This is due to the potential establishment of protective zones around offshore wind farm areas and submarine cable zones. Within the planned area, both active fishing methods, such as bottom trawling, pelagic trawling, and seine nets, which involve dragging gear across the seabed or through the water, and passive methods, such as gillnets, entangling nets, and other fish traps that capture passing fish, are currently employed.

We believes it may still be possible to use passive gear like nets and other traps in the wind farm zones, as these methods are not subject to regulations protecting submarine cables and pipelines. However, fishing with bottom-towed gear and pelagic trawls would be excluded from the protective zones. Consequently, fishers using these gear types would be displaced from these areas.

Currently, the intensity of fishing activities within the planned areas using such methods is not very high. As a result, the impact on this segment of commercial fishing is assessed as moderate and not significant.

2114. ID: 4550
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Radar and radio communication are critical for civil and military purposes at sea and in the airspace. Offshore wind farms and other marine structures may potentially affect radar coverage and radio communication, including radio link systems, if positioned within their coverage areas. Radar and radio waves can be reflected or weakened, degrading the signals.

The weather radar on Bornholm is the only civilian radar system that could be impacted by offshore wind farms planned in the area. The impact could result in a radar shadow zone behind the wind turbines, where radar signals are disrupted, appearing as 'clutter' on the screen. This will moderately affect the radar system, but the overall impact is assessed as not significant.

Potential disruptions from offshore wind farms are expected to have minimal impact on the quality of coastal radio systems, as these systems do not rely on a single line-of-sight connection. Therefore, the impact on radio systems is considered insignificant.

The implementation of the plan may temporarily block the line of sight between two receivers in the Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS), leading to momentary signal degradation. This could delay the correction of a ship’s GPS position (which has an accuracy of ~10 meters, compared to ~0.1 meters for DGPS). However, this impact on telecommunication, VHF, and navigation systems is assessed as insignificant.

Military radar systems are not included in the environmental assessment. The Ministry of Defense is conducting a separate analysis regarding these systems.

The choice of production capacity configuration for offshore wind energy does not affect these conclusions.

2115. ID: 4551
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The plan for the Energy Island at Bornholm may impact the exploration and extraction of marine raw materials if the designated areas overlap with resource zones. According to cable regulations, there is a general prohibition on raw material extraction within 200 meters on either side of seabed cables. As a result, the installation of seabed cables could affect raw material interests. 

There are deposits of raw materials of potential extraction interest within the park area and cable corridor. Allocating areas for seabed cables will create a protection zone where raw material extraction is prohibited. While this impact could be significant for specific areas, it is assessed that the plan area can be adjusted, or guidelines can be established to ensure that future projects do not conflict with raw material interests or only have minimal impact. 

The potential impact affects only a small number of resource deposits and is therefore assessed to be local in scope, permanent in duration, and low in intensity. The resource is not considered vulnerable, as similar resources can be extracted from other areas. For these reasons, the degree of impact is assessed as insignificant, and the overall effect is deemed not substantial.

They propose that Denmark could instead rely on green technologies, such as wind and solar energy, to ensure energy security without continuing fossil fuel production.

Despite this, Minister Dan Jørgensen maintains that Denmark has already set ambitious goals and is pushing for other countries to follow suit in establishing clear targets for phasing out fossil fuels. He emphasizes that Denmark's current stance and action plan are consistent with the global need for climate action, while calling for others to adopt similar measures in order to meet global climate targets.

2157. ID: 7081
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Beirut International
   Statement: Offshore wind energy generation is more efficient than on land, to harness it you’d have to follow the wind. Ocean water currents offer a much higher energy density, at a stable rate, the technology is progressing, to harness you’d have to follow the currents. 
To make Hydrogen Green, sea water reverse osmosis and electrolysis equipment have to be close to an energy source, from here the idea of Energy Islands begins. 

Energy Islands should be near the winds, waves and currents. The Baltic Sea average depth is 50 m, the North Sea 90 m, the Mediterranean Sea 1,500 m, the Atlantic Ocean 3,600 m.

Energy Islands should be accessible all year long. Offshore rigs personnel have to go through extensive safety training to be allowed to make the trip by Helicopter or by Offshore Support Vessels, both ways are expensive and at high risk.
Energy Islands should cater for additional space when an Wind Farm expands; and permit ergonomic maintenance and replacement of equipment without the use of heavy lift Floating Marine Cranes and Floating Docks.

Energy Islands service and operations teams may range from dozens to hundreds. This team require fresh water supply, food supply, cold service water, hot service water, wastewater disposal, solid waste disposal and regular rotation.  Offshore supply and retrieval trips made by Offshore Supply Vessels is dangerous and expensive in high seas.

Supposing a nation wishes to build an Energy Island by backfilling into the sea within its economic water zone; the currents within this sea would have to be studied not to alter direction and affect neighboring nations, the sediments from the backfilling process would be carried to undesirable locations within the nation shoreline, or to neighboring shoreline, affecting marine fauna and flora. A thorough Environmental Impact Assessment should be endorsed by all nation stakeholders.
Assuming an EIA is approved, lets look at the backfilling process on a sandy bed at 50 m seawater depth. If the surface footprint of the island is to be 500m x 500m, the scour protection measures, whatever the method used, would have a footprint of around 600m x 600m at sea bed level. The offshore contracting operations would have to be carried out within the yearly calm season, if the entire operation, or the milestone target construction is not achieved within the first season, the sea would destroy and remove most of it before the next season.
 After completion, if a structural failure occurs, under rough sea conditions, repairs would have to wait till the calm season, at the risk of further uncontrollable damage.
Once such Energy Island is completed, installing equipment on top would follow any port procedures; if certain components need to be replaced, they would have to be lifted and transported onto a vessel.
While this enormous offshore marine contracting job maybe concluded at 50m depth, will let the reader imagine the 90m or 1,500m sea depth scenario feasibility.

A Floating Island is fabricated in a shipyard, launched to sea, tugged to the desired location, and anchored. The process is carried in a controlled environment, irrespective of sea state and sea depth.
While many Floating Island solutions are marketed, and most developers submitted their design to the UN Habitat in 2018 in a New York meeting, none of their literature is conclusive, most of it is at conceptual level. 
The only solution that passed Two Marine Societies design approval by Bureau Veritas  in 2005 and International Naval Survey Bureau in 2009, and a thorough Marine Society design, engineering, procurement and fabrication survey by INSB from 2009 till 2015 is the one made by Dr. Abdullah Daou, the founder of Beirut International Marine Industry and Commerce. 
Beirut International’s Floating Island first prototype was made in 1997, at a scale of 1:10 measuring 4m x 4m, was extensively tested in a make shift water basin, with better than expected stability results under high simulated waves condition.

In 2009 the fabrication of the first Floating Island made by Beirut International started in Lebanon. The substructure base 48m wide, by 76m long, 9m deep and weighing around 4,000 tons was being assembled in Tripoli Shipyard, while structural components where being fabricated in three other workshops in Lebanon by a team of 431 local technicians and engineers. 
While the fate of this structure was unfortunate, Ninety-Eight Million US Dollars were invested in the research, development and fabrication; a 70% completion rate was achieved, almost all drawings approved and stamped by INSB meeting SOLAS and other marine regulations. 
The learning curve is priceless. The technology is ready, far ahead of any contender. True, a full-scale prototype is yet to be made again and tested.


There is seven pros for building the energy islands.
A Floating Energy Island is modular, making it scalable to meet any Offshore Wind Farm expansion. If maintenance is requires, a module can be detached, tugged to a shipyard then re-connected.
The substructure of a Floating Energy Island is transparent to the sea, making it an artificial coral reef for marine life, and simultaneously providing anchoring points to install Water Current Energy makers. 
The waves are absorbed and damped by the Floating Energy Island, creating a calm water area at the rear port for Vessel to approach and dock at ease, allowing for safe and friendly access. 
Being a generator of Hydrogen, and having a large underwater space, it is an ideal location to develop sustainable fisheries, creating an additional export income.
Solid waste composting and wastewater treatment available technologies can make some agriculture a sustainable alternative to waste disposal.
The Hydrogen process being noiseless, and clean; a Yacht Club can be safe haven for yachts sailing across seas and oceans.

However the cons of building the islands are yet to be tested by our firm.

The Hydrogen Environment is relatively new. 
Stakeholders include: Shipping Companies, Energy Companies, Ports Logistics, Telecommunication, Reverse Osmosis Water Makers, Electroliser Makers, Wind Turbine makers, Wave Energy Makers, Current Energy Makers, Shipyards, Marine Offshore Contractors, Hydrogen Storage Solution Makers, Inverters, Controls, Aquaponics, Wastewater Treatment, Solid Waste Treatment… 
While some stakeholders are more advanced then the other, some at prototyping stage, other at maturity; a Floating Energy Island success needs their close collaboration. A fresh firm in the Legal field is trying to advise stakeholders to join efforts and Joint Venture to make such infrastructure and energy concepts a needed reality to meet a Marine Decarbonization.

2170. ID: 5275
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: German collaboration
   Actor: Energinet
   Statement: Denmark and Germany have signed a milestone agreement for Energy Island Bornholm, with Germany now investing in the infrastructure to transport electricity from Energy Island Bornholm to the German market via an undersea power cable running from Bornholm's high-voltage facility to Germany.

Energinet and German transmission operator 50Hertz will each cover half of the infrastructure costs for the project and equally share the renewable energy portions generated by the project. The two operators will also equally distribute the congestion income from the power connections between the countries.

Beyond financial commitments, Germany is taking on partial responsibility for Energy Island Bornholm. Energinet and 50Hertz are not only initiating pioneering technical work - negotiations between the two companies and governments have also clarified ownership structures and distribution of energy quantities that can contribute to both countries' renewable energy goals.

This formalization of German involvement in Energy Island Bornholm, which was initially arranged in August 2022, was completed when Danish Climate Minister Lars Aagaard and German Economy Minister Robert Habeck signed the agreement at the European energy ministers' meeting in Luxembourg. This agreement represents a crucial cornerstone for Energy Island Bornholm.

   Year: 2023

   Statement: The agreement signed by Danish Climate Minister Lars Aagaard and German Economy Minister Robert Habeck in Luxembourg represents a crucial step for Denmark and Energinet. The development of very large offshore wind farms and international connections is vital for Denmark's political ambitions to export both green electricity and green hydrogen through future hydrogen pipelines in Denmark. The joint project in the Baltic Sea, together with Energinet's North Sea projects, will significantly impact Europe's green transition. The cooperation with German transmission operator 50Hertz on Energy Island Bornholm marks a shift away from point-to-point connections between individual countries. In the future, offshore wind power will flow to where demand is highest through offshore high-voltage direct current networks.

Energy Island Bornholm will create another trading connection between the German and Danish electricity markets. This is economically feasible and will increase both countries' security of supply under new geopolitical circumstances. The expansion of large offshore wind farms and international connections aligns with political ambitions and plans to export green energy, supporting the broader European green transition.

2173. ID: 5270

   Actor: Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply
   Statement: The Energy Island project in the North Sea has encountered a significant setback. The release of tender materials, initially planned before the summer, has been delayed. Current estimates from the Danish Energy Agency indicate that the project’s state costs exceed 50 billion kroner, making the project far from economically viable—a key condition in the political agreements underpinning the initiative.

The concept of energy islands, established in a political climate agreement, involves creating hubs to collect and distribute electricity generated by offshore wind turbines located far from land. The North Sea Energy Island is planned to be situated 80–100 kilometers off the west coast of Jutland.

Despite these challenges, the government remains committed to the ambition of establishing the North Sea Energy Island. However, due to the project’s high costs and significant risks, alternative approaches must be explored to ensure economic viability. In its current form, the project is not financially sustainable.

2222. ID: 4583
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: On Bornholm, it is assessed that high-voltage installations can be placed within the planned areas without damaging breeding and resting habitats for amphibians. Similarly, the installation of land cables will not harm amphibian breeding areas, as the cables will be drilled under lakes and streams as described in section 5.2. The landing of sea cables will also be done by drilling under coastal cliffs, thereby avoiding any potential damage to breeding and resting sites along the coast.

Within the planned area for land cables in Zealand, several waterholes are identified as potential breeding sites for Annex IV amphibians, such as agile frogs, common spadefoot toads, and great crested newts. It is assessed that it will be possible to avoid locations with Annex IV amphibian occurrences. Since soft soil areas and water-covered land will also be drilled under, no direct impact on the waterholes or breeding areas of these species is expected.

Based on the current knowledge, it is therefore assessed that the implementation of the Plan for the Energy Island Bornholm Program will not damage the breeding and resting habitats of amphibians protected under Annex IV.

2227. ID: 4580
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We emphasize that species listed under Annex IV of the EU Habitats Directive are subject to strict protection throughout the EU. These Annex IV species must not be disturbed, killed, or have their breeding and resting habitats damaged. Some of these species are common in Denmark, while others are rarer. Within the planning areas for the Energy Island projects and a 2 km buffer zone surrounding them, surveys have identified the presence of Annex IV species. Certain species, such as amphibians, are known to migrate between breeding ponds and resting areas.

The environmental assessment for the Plan for the Energy Island project at Bornholm includes evaluations of both potential temporary and permanent impacts, including physical interventions. These potential impacts are expected to arise from the temporary or permanent use of land and activities associated with the construction of high-voltage installations, as well as the burial and horizontal directional drilling of cables.

The surveys have recorded the following Annex IV species on Zealand: great crested newt, agile frog, common frog, viviparous lizard, and green hawker dragonfly, along with several bat species. On Bornholm, the species recorded include the great diving beetle, viviparous lizard, tree frog, natterjack toad, and common frog.

2228. ID: 4579
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: To implement the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm, cables may need to be installed through three Natura 2000 areas on land: N148 Køge Å, N149 Tryggevælde Å, and N187 Kystskrænter ved Arnager Bugt. A significance assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential impacts on these areas.

All cable installations within Natura 2000 areas will use guided horizontal drilling. The only potential impact identified is the risk of unintended drilling mud leaks. The significance assessment concludes that a significant impact on the designation basis of Natura 2000 area N187 can be ruled out because the habitat types within the area are not vulnerable to such leaks. Similarly, most habitat types and species in areas N148 and N149 are not vulnerable, but potential impacts on nutrient-rich lake habitats in N148 and lagoon habitats in N149 cannot be ruled out. Consequently, an impact assessment was conducted for these two habitat types.

Since the identified vulnerable habitats are small and located on the edges of the plan area, potential damage can be avoided by conducting drilling outside these sensitive habitats. The conclusion of the impact assessment is that the realization of the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm, either individually or in combination with other projects, will not risk harming the habitat types in the Natura 2000 designation basis. This is contingent on implementing all relevant mitigation measures in future projects. Based on this, the integrity of the Natura 2000 areas will not be compromised by the implementation of the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm on land.

2251. ID: 4589
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Technical University of Denmark
   Statement: Fortunately, the potential for wind power in the open sea is vast. However, the technical concept used for wind farms near the coast will not work in the open sea. For the near-shore parks we know today, the electricity is produced as alternating current (AC), which is transmitted directly through cables to the grid on land. The distance to parks in open water means that the electricity must be converted to direct current (DC) in order to be sent to land. The equipment responsible for converting the electricity – so-called converters – is so large that a physical structure is needed close to the production site. In other words, without energy islands, it will not be possible to expand offshore wind power on the scale that has been planned.

An added benefit is that there may be opportunities to place other types of production on the islands. This could include the production of hydrogen or green fuels for aviation, industry, heavy traffic, and shipping. This is also known as Power-to-X. The production of such fuels is a necessary condition for achieving the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global average temperature changes to no more than just under two degrees, or preferably no more than 1.5 degrees.

2269. ID: 6566
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Halonen et al.
   Statement: Norway's approach to energy transition presents a unique paradox. As a wealthy petro-state with strong social welfare systems, we've integrated sustainable development into our policies, but we haven't specifically tackled just transition in our energy policy discussions. Our welfare state heavily depends on petroleum revenues, and many assume our Oil Fund will simply carry us through the energy transition smoothly.

This assumption is problematic. We need to recognize that even wealthy Norway requires careful attention to justice in energy and climate policies. Currently, our just transition discussions are fragmented - they either focus solely on the oil and gas industry's needs or on specific communities' renewable energy projects. Instead, we need comprehensive national policies that address multiple aspects of justice: distributive, procedural, recognitive, and restorative.

Just as we've made sustainable development and SDGs fundamental to energy system planning, just transition principles need to be embedded at every policy level. This means expanding our focus on social aspects through community engagement in formal project development processes. The Storheia case demonstrates why we need participatory political processes that truly value local perspectives. However, we haven't yet realized the potential to address just transition at higher policymaking levels across multiple domains. Studying controversies can help us identify both the commonly addressed and neglected aspects of just transition, which should inform future policy development.

2304. ID: 869
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Journalist
   Statement: While researchers may calculate that it is theoretically possible to base energy supply on wind and solar power, I believe it is not desirable for several reasons.

First, there will inevitably be numerous challenges in translating theory into practice, leading to delays in the energy transition and prolonged dependence on fossil fuels.

Second, Power-to-X technology is not yet mature, and there are no facilities currently capable of delivering the scale of energy needed to power an entire country. Politicians are gambling on the rapid development of this technology, but there is no guarantee it will be ready when needed. Additionally, storing and transporting large quantities of energy for periods with no wind or solar power—such as calm, foggy weeks in January—presents significant logistical challenges.

The North Sea Energy Island is projected to cost 210 billion kroner, providing an installed capacity of 3 GW of wind turbines, with an actual average output of 1.5 GW due to a capacity factor of 50%. This must cover electricity consumption, Power-to-X needs, and electrified district heating. The Energy Island is not expected to be operational until 2033. By comparison, Poland has agreed to purchase six APR 1400 nuclear reactors from South Korea’s Kepco for 202 billion kroner, providing 8.4 GW installed capacity and 7.98 GW effective output due to a 95% capacity factor. The first reactor is expected to deliver electricity to the Polish grid by 2030. Nuclear power can also provide district heating, reducing the need for additional electricity. Given Denmark’s energy needs of 4–5 GW, the Polish model would offer surplus capacity for exports, synthetic fuels, or cost savings by building fewer reactors.

A wind- and solar-powered grid would require substantial technological solutions, such as using electric vehicle batteries to buffer fluctuations. A stable supply from nuclear power would eliminate the need for these costly and unnecessary innovations, reduce wear on expensive batteries, and avoid changing consumption habits—arguably one of the most challenging tasks.

It has been documented that wind power requires more than twice the resources (concrete, steel, copper, etc.) to deliver the same amount of energy as nuclear power.

Denmark currently imports hydropower from Norway during shortages, but Norway has faced decreasing rainfall in recent years, limiting its ability to export electricity. Norwegian energy officials have also stated that Norway neither can nor wishes to serve as a buffer for Northern Europe. Even Norway is debating nuclear power due to doubts about the long-term reliability of hydropower.

In summary, while it might be theoretically possible to rely on wind and solar power, I do not believe there is sufficient time to develop, build, and implement the necessary solutions or to change consumption habits. This approach risks prolonging our reliance on fossil fuels such as coal or deforestation-based biomass.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2308. ID: 2143
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Center for Regional and Tourism Research
   Statement: The construction of Energy Island Bornholm will require significant construction work, necessitating the temporary accommodation of a large workforce. It is not yet clear how the various contractors will address this need. We estimate approximately 5,300 annual work units of temporary labor will be involved in the construction phase of Energy Island Bornholm. This employment is not permanent but is noteworthy because it generates consumption linked to these work units, creating additional turnover on Bornholm and fostering local employment.
The temporary workforce will exhibit a consumption level and pattern different from that of the permanent residents and the typical Bornholm tourist. This workforce is expected to spend on daily goods, retail products, entertainment, dining, transportation, and similar services. However, it remains difficult to determine the exact local spending levels. 
Based on SKAT’s tax deduction guidelines for dual household maintenance during work assignments, we have assumed an average daily expenditure of 555 DKK per person as a baseline consumption estimate. Over the construction period, this workforce is projected to spend a total of 662 million DKK. The impact of this spending is referred to as temporary, derived employment in our tables and graphs, resulting in an additional 135 annual work units of local employment.

2309. ID: 2141
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Center for Regional and Tourism Research
   Statement: Energy Island Bornholm is expected to generate new jobs and population growth on Bornholm. Our calculations show that the impact will be minimal if Bornholm only serves as a service port for the energy island and maximal if a Power-to-X (PtX) facility is also established. Approximately half of the new jobs and population increase associated with Energy Island Bornholm will only materialize if a PtX facility, based on a 3GW hydrogen production plant, is constructed. 
A PtX facility would also create localized by-products, such as surplus heat, which could attract new businesses that utilize this surplus heat in their operations. These additional socioeconomic effects have not been included in our current calculations and should be added to the presented figures. The dimensions of the calculated PtX facility are based on the original plans associated with two open-door projects already underway on Bornholm. Other effects of these open-door projects were not included in this analysis. 
Based on experience from Energy Island calculations, we estimate that fully realizing the open-door projects would lead to an additional 590 new residents, resulting in a total migration increase of over 1,600 individuals if both the energy island and open-door projects are implemented. If the electricity from the energy island is used for PtX production, the total migration is expected to be approximately 1,060 individuals. However, this estimate does not include potential employment and migration resulting from the greening of Bornholm’s economy or the emergence of new green industries. These effects are addressed in a separate report focusing on the further development of Bornholm as a testing hub for energy technology.

2331. ID: 2691
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The Climate, Energy, and Utilities Committee has asked me, in a letter dated June 1, 2023, to answer the following question, which was requested by Steffen W. Frølund (LA). The question concerns the consequences of applying the same tariff model, expected to be used for Energiø Bornholm, to all renewable energy (RE) electricity producers connected at the transmission level.

I must first note that according to the market directive, it is the collective electricity supply companies that develop tariff methods, and the Energy Regulatory Authority (Forsyningstilsynet) that approves them. This means that the Minister or the Parliament has very limited ability to dictate tariff designs.

The tariff pricing methods must, among other things, adhere to the principle of cost-reflectiveness, meaning they must reflect the costs incurred by the various categories of network users. In connection with this, Energinet has informed me that the general tariff model for producer payments specifically excludes electricity production connected to energy islands. This is because the standardized connection fee now applied for electricity production cannot, in a cost-reflective manner, accommodate the payment required for connection to energy islands. The transmission network at and near energy islands is of a special nature, as it includes both trade connections to foreign countries and specialized installations for connecting offshore wind, which also involves significantly higher investment costs compared to, for example, the connection of a typical offshore wind farm or larger solar park.

As a result, Energinet is currently developing a tariff financing model for Energinet’s costs related to energy islands. This model was sent for public consultation on May 3, 2023, with a response deadline of June 6, 2023. The draft tariff model proposes that the offshore wind connected to an energy island will be tariffed according to the costs it incurs. This draft includes, among other things, that electricity producers and consumers will share the financing of parts of Energinet’s costs using a distribution key specially developed for financing Energinet’s costs related to energy islands in order to allocate these costs in a cost-reflective manner.

Such a distribution key cannot be applied to tariffing other RE electricity producers, as they do not contribute to the financing of trade connections as part of their connection to the grid. This is because other RE electricity producers are not directly dependent on specific trade connections in their grid connection and the sale of their production, like the offshore wind connected at Energiø Bornholm.

2363. ID: 5711
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: ELECTA research group
   Statement: We conducted a preliminary assessment of the concept for a Mediterranean energy island in Sardinia, linking Italy, France, and Spain with HVDC interconnections. Our initial findings indicate significant benefits for Europe, including reduced operational costs and lower CO2 emissions for the DE and GA scenarios of ENTSO-E’s TYNDP. Using a European nodal model, we observed even greater benefits in terms of operational costs and CO2 emissions, as the investment also alleviates internal grid congestion.

We performed a preliminary economic assessment of the investment costs for the entire energy island. The estimated costs range from 5.98 billion to 7.04 billion euros for 1 GW HVDC links and from 11.96 billion to 19.53 billion euros for 2 GW HVDC links, which are comparable to current projects. However, a case-specific investigation is necessary for more accurate figures.

Future work will include detailed nodal simulations for Sardinia’s and Corsica’s grids, additional scenarios, more planning years, and the option to run OPFs for selected market zones. We will also develop more risk-aware power flow control simulations to account for potential HVDC link faults. Planned refinements include Security-constrained Optimal Power Flow, unbalanced operation of bipolar HVDC links, and topological actions for meshed AC/DC grids.

2372. ID: 2866

   Statement: We plan to introduce a new electricity price zone for Bornholm to address the challenges and opportunities created by the Energy Island project. This includes integrating up to 3 GW of offshore wind energy and connecting directly to Germany and Sjælland. By creating this new zone, we can ensure that market mechanisms reflect the capacity constraints of the cables, preventing inefficiencies and high costs from countertrading.

If no such connection is established due to complexity or cost, Bornholm will remain part of the existing eastern Denmark (DK2) price zone, and an offshore price zone will instead cover only the wind farms and island infrastructure. In this scenario, Bornholm would continue to rely solely on its cable connection to Sweden.  

The purpose of the new price zone is to make the limitations of the transmission capacity between Bornholm, Zealand, and Germany visible to the market. Without this, the market could mistakenly assume that unlimited energy transfers are possible, leading to imbalances and costly corrective measures for Energinet, and by extension, the Danish public.  

The expected price benefit arises from market mechanisms where Bornholm’s spot price will align with the lowest neighboring price—either Zealand’s or Germany’s—depending on capacity availability. However, the price differences between these regions are usually minor. Under normal circumstances, the spot price only constitutes about 23% of the total consumer electricity bill, with taxes and tariffs making up the majority. Therefore, a lower wholesale price will only marginally impact overall consumer costs.  

Certain conditions, such as maintenance or cable damage, could cause energy production to exceed cable capacity, leading to temporarily lower prices on Bornholm. Conversely, if offshore wind production is low and cables are fully utilized, Bornholm’s price could match the higher German rates.  

Ultimately, the effect of a new price zone will depend on the evolving structure of the Energy Island project, such as additional wind capacity or the construction of large electricity-consuming facilities like power-to-X plants, which could either decrease or increase local electricity prices accordingly.

not work for an open sea park. Due to the longer
distance, the power must be converted into a
direct current (DC). The space requirements for the
converters and related equipment demand housing
at a physical structure close to the production site.
In other words, a build-out of the scale in question
would be impossible without energy islands.

We further acknowledge the cooperation established between Denmark, Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands in the “Esbjerg Declaration” of May 18th, 2022, which envisions the North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe. In our view, offshore renewable energy hubs and a meshed offshore grid are essential for generating, connecting, converting, and transporting offshore wind energy in the North Sea. 

We note Germany’s plans to establish offshore renewable energy clusters with a 10 GW capacity in the North Sea by the mid-2030s and Denmark’s plans to create a Danish Energy Island with up to 10 GW capacity by 2040. Additionally, we recall the EU Marine Strategy Directive and our joint commitment to achieving good environmental status for all European seas, including the North Sea.

We have agreed on the necessity of this Joint Declaration of Intent (JDoI) to focus on cooperation for connecting Germany’s planned offshore renewable energy hubs with Denmark’s Energy Island. Our primary objective is to facilitate mutual benefits by improving energy security, increasing socio-economic welfare, diversifying energy sources, meeting EU and national renewable energy targets, and integrating wind power with hydrogen and Power-to-X technologies.

To achieve this, we propose the establishment of a Joint Working Group led by energy ministries, supported by energy authorities and Transmission System Operators (TSOs). This group will develop a pre-feasibility study analyzing technical, environmental, and economic aspects and deliver a joint recommendation by the first half of 2024. This recommendation will guide the next steps toward realizing the project, aiming for implementation by the mid-2030s.

We emphasize that this JDoI creates no binding obligations under international law and imposes no financial commitments unless mutually agreed. Cooperation costs are borne by the respective Participant. Any amendments to this JDoI require joint written consent, and any misunderstandings will be resolved collaboratively in good faith and mutual trust. 

This JDoI takes effect upon signature and may be terminated with three months' written notice. Termination does not affect ongoing activities unless otherwise decided.

Signed on April 24th, 2023, in Ostende.

2455. ID: 2296
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Financial viability and (un)profitability
   Actor: John Ammentorp
   Statement: Energy islands are strategically vital and economically sound investments for several key reasons. The Danish North Sea energy island project will make energy more affordable by creating near-shore environments for far-offshore wind farms. By placing wind farms closer to energy islands instead of the mainland, the Danish North Sea energy island will reduce complexity and costs by minimizing or eliminating long underwater cable runs to shore.

Energy islands provide crucial flexibility in Denmark's renewable energy system. The Danish North Sea energy island will serve as an accumulation point for surplus energy during high-production periods and enable strategic distribution during peak demand times. This capability directly addresses the challenge of balancing renewable energy production with consumption.

The costs for the Danish North Sea energy island fall into three main categories:
1. Capital expenditures for physical infrastructure construction, including the artificial island itself and electrical infrastructure
2. Operational costs that vary based on design choices, technology selection, geographic location, and project scale
3. Technology development costs, particularly for high-voltage direct current equipment and Power-to-X systems

2460. ID: 985
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Diogo da Conceição Rego
   Statement: Here’s a more concise version using “I”:

Power-to-X (PtX) refers to technologies that convert surplus renewable electricity into other forms of energy, such as green hydrogen, ammonia, or synthetic fuels. I see the ramp-up of the PtX industry as a key opportunity to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, create jobs, improve energy security, and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

However, I recognize that several challenges remain before PtX can be widely adopted. The industry's products are still more expensive than fossil fuel alternatives, and regulatory and market uncertainties hinder the signing of long-term contracts, creating a "chicken-egg" dilemma.

To accelerate the global energy transition, H2Global was established as a funding mechanism for PtX projects outside the EU. With initial funding from the German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action (BMWK), H2Global aims to kick-start global trade in PtX products like green ammonia and e-methanol.

Focusing on financing challenges, I note that financial institutions are still cautious in their engagement with PtX projects, often limited to grants and feasibility studies. PtX projects are capital-intensive and require substantial funding, with the need for financial institutions to offer significant leverage and extended tenors.

The novelty of PtX demands innovative business models, such as the “Captive Model” (on-site production for self-consumption) and the “Merchant Model” (production for sale), which impact risks and cash flow. PtX projects involve multiple stages, and investments may need to be bundled or separated into distinct projects, each requiring tailored financing mechanisms.

Investors face challenges due to market uncertainties, technological risks, and logistical concerns. Strong government support and de-risking instruments, such as first-loss guarantees, are crucial for enhancing project bankability. Additionally, concessional loans and grants can help attract equity providers, especially for early-stage projects.

I believe that PtX projects’ competitiveness will be shaped by factors such as remuneration for production, risk mitigation, and the establishment of a global PtX-finance knowledge hub. H2Global can play a key role in setting standards for PtX fuel auctions, and collaborative efforts to reduce risk perception could accelerate industry growth.

In conclusion, by addressing these challenges and leveraging governmental support and innovative financing mechanisms, I am confident that PtX projects can accelerate the transition to a greener energy future.

2485. ID: 6089
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Beirut International
   Statement: ACTOR:
Beirut International - Marine Industry and Commerce sarl

CONTROVERSY:
The Danish “Energy Island” projects

TEXT:
Offshore wind energy generation is more efficient than on land, to harness it you’d have to follow the wind. Ocean water currents offer a much higher energy density, at a stable rate, the technology is progressing, to harness you’d have to follow the currents. 
To make Hydrogen Green, sea water reverse osmosis and electrolysis equipment have to be close to an energy source, from here the idea of Energy Islands begins. 

Energy Islands should be near the winds, waves and currents. The Baltic Sea average depth is 50 m, the North Sea 90 m, the Mediterranean Sea 1,500 m, the Atlantic Ocean 3,600 m.

Energy Islands should be accessible all year long. Offshore rigs personnel have to go through extensive safety training to be allowed to make the trip by Helicopter or by Offshore Support Vessels, both ways are expensive and at high risk.
Energy Islands should cater for additional space when an Wind Farm expands; and permit ergonomic maintenance and replacement of equipment without the use of heavy lift Floating Marine Cranes and Floating Docks.

Energy Islands service and operations teams may range from dozens to hundreds. This team require fresh water supply, food supply, cold service water, hot service water, wastewater disposal, solid waste disposal and regular rotation.  Offshore supply and retrieval trips made by Offshore Supply Vessels is dangerous and expensive in high seas.

Supposing a nation wishes to build an Energy Island by backfilling into the sea within its economic water zone; the currents within this sea would have to be studied not to alter direction and affect neighboring nations, the sediments from the backfilling process would be carried to undesirable locations within the nation shoreline, or to neighboring shoreline, affecting marine fauna and flora. A thorough Environmental Impact Assessment should be endorsed by all nation stakeholders.
Assuming an EIA is approved, lets look at the backfilling process on a sandy bed at 50 m seawater depth. If the surface footprint of the island is to be 500m x 500m, the scour protection measures, whatever the method used, would have a footprint of around 600m x 600m at sea bed level. The offshore contracting operations would have to be carried out within the yearly calm season, if the entire operation, or the milestone target construction is not achieved within the first season, the sea would destroy and remove most of it before the next season.
 After completion, if a structural failure occurs, under rough sea conditions, repairs would have to wait till the calm season, at the risk of further uncontrollable damage.
Once such Energy Island is completed, installing equipment on top would follow any port procedures; if certain components need to be replaced, they would have to be lifted and transported onto a vessel.
While this enormous offshore marine contracting job maybe concluded at 50m depth, will let the reader imagine the 90m or 1,500m sea depth scenario feasibility.

A Floating Island is fabricated in a shipyard, launched to sea, tugged to the desired location, and anchored. The process is carried in a controlled environment, irrespective of sea state and sea depth.
While many Floating Island solutions are marketed, and most developers submitted their design to the UN Habitat in 2018 in a New York meeting, none of their literature is conclusive, most of it is at conceptual level. 
The only solution that passed Two Marine Societies design approval by Bureau Veritas  in 2005 and International Naval Survey Bureau in 2009, and a thorough Marine Society design, engineering, procurement and fabrication survey by INSB from 2009 till 2015 is the one made by Dr. Abdullah Daou, the founder of Beirut International Marine Industry and Commerce. 
Beirut International’s Floating Island first prototype was made in 1997, at a scale of 1:10 measuring 4m x 4m, was extensively tested in a make shift water basin, with better than expected stability results under high simulated waves condition.

In 2009 the fabrication of the first Floating Island made by Beirut International started in Lebanon. The substructure base 48m wide, by 76m long, 9m deep and weighing around 4,000 tons was being assembled in Tripoli Shipyard, while structural components where being fabricated in three other workshops in Lebanon by a team of 431 local technicians and engineers. 
While the fate of this structure was unfortunate, Ninety-Eight Million US Dollars were invested in the research, development and fabrication; a 70% completion rate was achieved, almost all drawings approved and stamped by INSB meeting SOLAS and other marine regulations. 
The learning curve is priceless. The technology is ready, far ahead of any contender. True, a full-scale prototype is yet to be made again and tested.


There is seven pros for building the energy islands.
A Floating Energy Island is modular, making it scalable to meet any Offshore Wind Farm expansion. If maintenance is requires, a module can be detached, tugged to a shipyard then re-connected.
The substructure of a Floating Energy Island is transparent to the sea, making it an artificial coral reef for marine life, and simultaneously providing anchoring points to install Water Current Energy makers. 
The waves are absorbed and damped by the Floating Energy Island, creating a calm water area at the rear port for Vessel to approach and dock at ease, allowing for safe and friendly access. 
Being a generator of Hydrogen, and having a large underwater space, it is an ideal location to develop sustainable fisheries, creating an additional export income.
Solid waste composting and wastewater treatment available technologies can make some agriculture a sustainable alternative to waste disposal.
The Hydrogen process being noiseless, and clean; a Yacht Club can be safe haven for yachts sailing across seas and oceans.

However the cons of building the islands are yet to be tested by our firm.

The Hydrogen Environment is relatively new. 
Stakeholders include: Shipping Companies, Energy Companies, Ports Logistics, Telecommunication, Reverse Osmosis Water Makers, Electroliser Makers, Wind Turbine makers, Wave Energy Makers, Current Energy Makers, Shipyards, Marine Offshore Contractors, Hydrogen Storage Solution Makers, Inverters, Controls, Aquaponics, Wastewater Treatment, Solid Waste Treatment… 
While some stakeholders are more advanced then the other, some at prototyping stage, other at maturity; a Floating Energy Island success needs their close collaboration. A fresh firm in the Legal field is trying to advise stakeholders to join efforts and Joint Venture to make such infrastructure and energy concepts a needed reality to meet a Marine Decarbonization.

2508. ID: 2593
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Peter K. Kruse-Andersena
   Statement: I highlight a coordination problem between the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy, using Denmark's planned North Sea energy island as an example. The long gap between the project's announcement and its start in 2033 could lead to a 'Green Paradox,' where emissions actually increase in the EU ETS due to the way the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) functions. My study shows that the leakage rate in 2050 could be as high as 145%, and I suggest potential solutions to improve the climate benefits of large-scale projects like this. These include revising the EU ETS or utilizing Power-to-X technologies, though these won't fully resolve the coordination failure. One option is removing the MSR or adjusting the emission cap to give politicians more control over long-term emissions, but this could increase leakage effects and price volatility. In conclusion, there is no easy solution to this problem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2510. ID: 2607
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: M. P. van der Laan, O. García-Santiago, N. N. Sørensen, N. Troldborg, J. Criado Risco and J. Badger
   Statement: Our research team has conducted a comprehensive comparison of five different models to simulate wind farm interactions in the Danish Energy Island cluster. Our findings reveal significant limitations in the PARK1 model, which only shows a 5.7% Annual Energy Production wake loss and fails to capture wind farm interactions. In contrast, our other models (RANS-LUT, RANS-AWF, RANS-AD, and WRF) consistently predict higher wake losses between 8.6-10.1%, indicating that wind farm interactions effectively eliminate the output of one entire wind farm out of ten.

Based on these findings, we strongly advocate for exploring alternative wind farm layouts and cluster configurations to minimize these losses. Specifically, we suggest investigating irregular layouts and optimized placement strategies.

While implementing the RANS-AD method for large clusters presents challenges due to grid size requirements, we've successfully demonstrated its scalability up to 1024 Actuator Disks and grids of 1.26 billion cells using 4800 cores. For those seeking a more computationally efficient approach, we've found that the RANS-AWF method, when paired with lower-fidelity wake models, offers a viable alternative. Our RANS-LUT model has proven particularly accurate, achieving average absolute errors of just 0.94% for thrust coefficients and 1.4% for power coefficients across all wind directions at below-rated wind speeds.

We acknowledge certain limitations in our RANS models - they don't account for mesoscale effects and use a simplified inflow model without Atmospheric Boundary Layer height and Coriolis forces, due to numerical issues that warrant further study. However, we can confirm that our WRF mesoscale model's predictions of wind farm interaction align with those of our RANS models, validating our overall findings.

2512. ID: 2536
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Alexandra Lüth
   Statement: The currently envisioned technology for energy islands is prohibitively expensive compared to other flexible energy sources and conventional hydrogen production, primarily due to its technological immaturity. A viable mix of technologies is likely to emerge only if CO₂ or hydrogen prices increase or if technology costs decrease. Offshore electrolysers and energy islands represent a new, untested component within energy systems, which introduces significant risks. It is advisable that offshore electrolysers be constructed at moderate sizes and operated at a capacity factor of 50%. Furthermore, while high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables hold promise for offshore applications, they remain costly and require further testing as they are still in the early stages of development. The energy island projects are part of a large-scale rollout, making them inherently expensive and challenging. The advancement of technology will significantly influence the benefits and competitiveness of these systems, highlighting a trade-off between electricity and hydrogen supply.

This plan outlines the overall framework for establishing the project and its potential environmental impact. Currently, the Danish Energy Agency has sent the plan and environmental assessment into the second public consultation phase, which will last until December 1st. The plan is expected to be adopted early next year. The plan involves three key projects: offshore wind farms south and west of Bornholm, the cable connection to Germany developed by our German colleagues from 50Hertz Transmission GmbH, and Energinet's facilities, which include two converter stations on Bornholm and Zealand, and a 1.2 GW direct current connection between them. The environmental assessment, prepared with assistance from Øbisserne, provides a high-level overview of the potential environmental consequences of fully developing Energiø Bornholm, both at sea and on land. This assessment helps us understand how to best consider environmental factors during the construction of the energy island. I encourage everyone interested to review the consultation materials and submit feedback by December 1st on the Danish Energy Agency's website.

2568. ID: 5577
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Council on Climate Change
   Statement: Denmark can maintain high electricity supply security even under extreme weather conditions, despite the European electricity system increasingly relying on solar and wind energy. This security can be ensured through straightforward measures without significantly raising overall electricity supply costs. These measures include making electricity consumption more flexible, storing energy, and investing in reserve capacity for critical situations. 

However, the transformation of the energy system will place greater pressure on electricity supply security due to a significant increase in electricity consumption and the growing reliance on solar and wind energy, which cannot be regulated as easily as traditional power plants. By 2040, nearly all Danish electricity production will come from renewable sources, and electricity consumption will rise substantially, driven by national and EU policies to expand offshore wind and solar power while electrifying a significant portion of energy use. 

The challenges to electricity supply security are manageable, but implementing the necessary solutions—such as flexible consumption, energy storage, and reserve capacity—will take many years. Authorities must act promptly to address these challenges to avoid potential electricity shortages during peak demand periods when renewable sources cannot meet inflexible consumption. Ensuring supply security requires robust planning, including addressing reliance on varying energy sources, diminished dispatchable power plant capacity, and uncertain availability of electricity imports during stressed conditions.

2583. ID: 617
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We state that, as part of the Climate Agreement for energy and industry, Denmark has decided to develop two energy islands: one in the North Sea and one in the Baltic Sea near Bornholm. These energy islands are a key component of the expansion of offshore wind in both the North and Baltic Seas and are expected to play a significant role in Denmark's and Europe's green transition.

It has been politically decided that the Energy Island near Bornholm must be located at least 15 kilometers from the coast, with a minimum capacity of 3 GW of offshore wind power, with the potential for an additional 800 MW of overcapacity, bringing the total capacity to up to 3.8 GW.

The Energy Island near Bornholm will consist of offshore facilities in the Baltic Sea, including wind turbines with internal seabed cables, offshore transformer platforms, and seabed cables connecting the wind farms to Bornholm and from Bornholm to Zealand, as well as an international connection to Germany. On land, there will be land-based facilities on Bornholm (buried land cables and a high-voltage station) and in Solhøj, Zealand (buried land cables and a high-voltage station).

2595. ID: 5598
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: Yes, it is true that both Energinet and the agreement group have approved the possibility of Chinese cables being used in Denmark, but this is contingent on the fulfillment of specific requirements. The upcoming offshore wind auctions will allow both European and non-European companies, including Chinese companies, to participate, provided they meet the tender conditions. However, the actual suppliers of components, such as cables, are not part of the auction process. The winner of the auction (the concessionaire) can select their own suppliers, including those of cables, for the wind farm construction.

For the future wind auctions, there will be conditions that must be met, including new access requirements. These will include compliance with social clauses, such as the obligation to provide apprenticeship opportunities and prevent social dumping. Furthermore, there will be requirements to adhere to human rights and international conventions. The principle of chain responsibility will also be introduced, meaning that the concessionaire will be accountable for ensuring both their own compliance and that of their suppliers when working in Denmark. Additionally, sustainability requirements will be enforced, such as ensuring that concessionaires obtain third-party verified environmental product declarations for key components, including cables, from their suppliers.

   Statement: We believe it is crucial to balance urgency with wisdom in advancing the Danish 'Energy Island' projects. Some may worry that incorporating research into the process could delay construction, but we argue that research should run parallel to construction, interacting directly with the building and operational phases. This approach is unconventional and challenging, but the potential rewards are significant.

Past Danish projects integrating wind power into the energy system show how such research efforts have been essential in making renewable energy a major component of our energy supply. Similarly, lessons learned from the ongoing Bornholm energy island project in the Baltic Sea can directly inform the development of the artificial energy island in the North Sea.

To ensure the success of these initiatives, we propose two sets of actions. First, we recommend immediately implementing six specific initiatives in collaboration between industry and researchers. Second, we advocate for a comprehensive set of research efforts to generate insights that will continually enhance the design and operation of future energy islands.

This plan establishes the overall framework for the project's implementation and its potential environmental impacts. The Danish Energy Agency is now putting this plan and its environmental assessment into a second public consultation phase until December 1st, with the plan expected to be adopted in early next year.

The project consists of three main components:
1. Offshore wind farms south and west of Bornholm
2. A cable connection to Germany, being established by our German colleagues at 50Hertz Transmission GmbH
3. Energinet's facilities, which include two converter stations (one on Bornholm and one on Zealand) and a 1.2 GW DC connection between them

The Øbisserne team has assisted the Danish Energy Agency in preparing the environmental impact assessment that accompanies the Energy Island Bornholm plan, both for marine and land-based aspects. This assessment outlines the environmental consequences of a fully developed Energy Island Bornholm at a general level, helping us understand how to best consider environmental factors during construction.

All interested parties can access the consultation materials and submit responses until December 1st through the Danish Energy Agency's website.

2649. ID: 1916
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Energinet
   Statement: We ensure that onshore balancing and reserve dimensioning align with the System Operation Guideline (SOGL) at both the LFC block and LFC area levels. We plan to apply the same principles for dimensioning and balancing to the future Danish energy islands. This means that each energy island will function as a separate LFC area within the same LFC block as the connected Danish onshore LFC areas.

By designating the energy islands as individual LFC areas, we enhance transparency regarding bottlenecks between the islands and the mainland while reducing the need for internal redispatch. Reserve dimensioning remains at the LFC block level, and the SOGL imposes no restrictions on sharing or exchanging reserves between LFC areas within the same block. Including the energy islands in the existing LFC block enables common reserve dimensioning for both the islands and the connected Danish onshore LFC areas.

Additionally, establishing new LFC areas supports the seamless integration of energy islands into European balancing platforms. However, there are legal challenges, as current legislation was drafted before the concept of energy islands existed. We believe that energy islands can be balanced under existing regulations, but legislative amendments are needed to explicitly cover small, isolated AC systems like the energy islands.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2654. ID: 5694
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Andreas Wenzel
   Statement: The agreement encompasses a total of 9 gigawatts (GW) of offshore wind capacity, with the potential to expand to 14 GW or more. Currently, Denmark has 2.3 GW of offshore wind capacity in its waters. The agreement includes 6 GW of regular offshore wind farms and an additional 3 GW linked to the "Energy Island Bornholm Project." 

For the first time, the agreement establishes state co-ownership of offshore wind farms, with the Danish state and citizens holding a 20% stake. While this milestone is significant, it has sparked debates over the potential complexity and delays in the bidding process. The agreement sets a strict timeline for constructing the wind turbines by 2030.

The "Energy Island Bornholm Project" requires state support to be realized. Politicians have allocated up to 17.6 billion DKK in subsidies to cover the costs of an onshore facility on Bornholm and a high-capacity transmission cable connecting Bornholm, Zealand, and Germany. Germany will contribute its share and partially fund the onshore facility. However, the wind turbines themselves will be constructed without financial support.

This agreement represents a major step in the energy transition, ensuring the generation of significant amounts of green electricity for Denmark, Germany, and the rest of Europe.

There is a reason why we have chosen to live where we do. A strong economy with corresponding benefits could attract new residents, but a municipality that becomes a climate desert with vast areas covered in solar panels and wind turbines would have the opposite effect—driving people away. We must protect our beautiful landscape and nature. Right now, ideologies, nature, open spaces, and small communities are being sold to the highest bidder. There is so much money at stake that ordinary people cannot resist the temptation. I deeply understand this, but it is not beneficial for Lemvig Municipality, which has already taken its share of the Prime Minister’s goal of quadrupling wind energy. I believe the time has come for our municipality to truly experience the economic benefits if we are to see more renewable energy. After all, it is us who will have to live with it.

2703. ID: 5731
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Researchers
   Statement: Offshore wind, both fixed-bottom and floating, is crucial for the North Sea energy system, potentially contributing up to 51% of total power generation and reaching 498 GW of capacity by 2050. This technology also lowers the cumulative system cost of electricity and hydrogen by 4.21%. Fixed-bottom offshore wind will achieve 100% of its deployment potential regardless of technological learning and spatial planning. However, floating wind deployment is highly dependent on technological advancements, with potential capacities ranging from 117 to 276 GW.

Spatial planning is essential for maximizing fixed-bottom offshore wind deployment. Policymakers and industry must focus on commercializing floating wind technology within this decade. An integrated offshore grid is vital for optimizing floating wind deployment and its benefits in the North Sea system. Low-TRL offshore renewables, such as tidal stream, wave technology, and bioethanol, will play a limited role due to their higher costs compared to more mature technologies.

2711. ID: 5953
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Danish Energy Agency has reported on the socioeconomic impact assessments for different configurations of the Energy Island Bornholm under various scenarios. The Energy Island Bornholm project includes offshore wind farms, a transformer station on Bornholm, and grid connections to Denmark and Germany. Despite considerable uncertainty about future developments, the central socioeconomic estimates are negative across all scenarios, ranging from -4 billion DKK to -17 billion DKK.

The project is also expected to require public subsidies amounting to 31.5 billion DKK during the first approximately 20 years of the energy island's lifespan. Of this, 17.6 billion DKK was politically approved in May 2023. This approved subsidy will be financed through expected revenues from the auction of 6 GW offshore wind capacity (8.7 billion DKK), the Green Fund (4.9 billion DKK), and future fiscal space (4.0 billion DKK). An additional subsidy need of approximately 14 billion DKK has arisen due to the anticipated unprofitability of the offshore wind farms associated with the energy island, and no concrete financing has yet been identified for this amount.

Given the negative socioeconomic outlook, the Energy Island Bornholm project should be reconsidered. The socioeconomic assessment does not include several effects that are difficult to quantify, such as energy security and potential Power-to-X production. It is recommended that a comprehensive socioeconomic analysis be conducted, incorporating as many effects as possible. If it cannot be demonstrated that the project yields a socioeconomic surplus, the project should be abandoned.

   Statement: I hereby submit a legislative proposal to modify the investment screening law and gas supply law. The investment screening law changes introduce an earlier screening timeline for certain cases, specifically to enable greater parallel processing between the new EU foreign subsidy screening (FSR) and investment screening for offshore wind tenders and other major public energy projects.

These modifications are essential to avoid delays in upcoming tenders and reduce maintenance periods. For the investment screening law changes, adoption must occur in the current session to provide clarity to bidders and contracting authorities regarding the screening process and timing well before the bid deadlines for upcoming offshore wind tenders. This is particularly relevant as Energinet has already initiated tenders for electrical equipment for Energy Island Bornholm, with an expected bid deadline in autumn 2024.

Regarding the gas supply law changes, I propose introducing an explicit legal provision on the establishment and independence of the Energy Appeals Board to meet EU legal requirements under Article 41(17) of Directive 2009/73/EC and Article 60(8) of Directive (EU) 2019/944.

The proposal's late submission is due to the urgency of clarifying the screening process before the upcoming offshore wind tenders, including the already initiated Bornholm Energy Island electrical equipment tender. The law should enter into force on July 1, 2024.

This proposal does not entail significant economic consequences for businesses.

2746. ID: 6919
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Sairoel Amertet Finecomess
   Statement: The newest innovation in energy management on the demand side is the smart meter, which helps reduce energy waste, improve productivity, and lower costs by monitoring energy consumption in real time. Smart meters allow users to easily and quickly track their energy usage, making them an innovative tool for energy management. These devices measure energy consumption in homes or businesses and communicate with the energy source to send data to the energy supplier, ensuring accurate billing. They also record usage data over time, enabling users to monitor consumption patterns and take steps to reduce energy use when necessary.

Smart meters can measure electricity, water, and natural gas usage and are typically connected to a wireless network for real-time data collection and transmission. By monitoring energy use in different areas of a home or business, users can identify specific areas of high consumption and take action to save energy. 

Smart meters offer several advantages. They provide consumers with real-time insights into their energy consumption, enabling cost-saving measures. Energy providers can use the data collected to create detailed profiles of customer energy usage, allowing for better demand management and more personalized services. The widespread adoption of smart meters in many countries is driving improvements in energy systems, enhancing efficiency, and empowering consumers with greater control and awareness of their energy use.
